• Oxygen in potassium superoxide has an average oxidation state of \(-\frac{1}{2}\).
The correct combination is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q06 - Stoichiometric coefficients of water in balanced equations

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II to match each redox reaction with the coefficient and location of water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) in its balanced net ionic equation:

List-I (Redox Reaction System) List-II (Coefficient and Position of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\))
A. Oxidation of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) by \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) in acidic medium I. \(1\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side
B. Oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\) by \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) in acidic medium II. \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side
C. Oxidation of \(\mathrm{Br}^{-}\) by \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}\) in basic medium III. \(7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side
D. Oxidation of \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\) by \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}\) in basic medium to form \(\mathrm{I}_2\) and \(\mathrm{MnO}_2\) IV. \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dichromate oxidation of ferrous ion in acidic medium
The balanced reduction half-reaction is:
\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 14\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\).
The oxidation half-reaction is \(6\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 6\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{e}^-\).
Summing the half-reactions gives the overall balanced equation:
\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 14\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\).
This contains \(7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side.

Step 2: Dichromate oxidation of sulfite ion in acidic medium
The oxidation state of chromium decreases from \(+6\) to \(+3\) (\(\Delta = -3\) per Cr, total decrease of \(6\)). The oxidation state of sulfur increases from \(+4\) to \(+6\) (\(\Delta = +2\)). To equalize electron transfer, 3 sulfite ions react per dichromate ion:
\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 3\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 8\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 3\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\).
This contains \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side.

Step 3: Permanganate oxidation of bromide ion in basic medium
Permanganate is reduced from \(+7\) to \(+4\) (\(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), decrease of \(3\)). Bromide is oxidised from \(-1\) to \(+5\) in bromate (\(\mathrm{BrO}_3^-\), increase of \(6\)). Balancing changes gives a mole ratio of \(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) to \(1\mathrm{Br}^-\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Br}^-(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{BrO}_3^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{OH}^-(\mathrm{aq})\).
This contains \(1\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side.

Step 4: Permanganate oxidation of iodide ion in basic medium
The balanced half-reactions in basic medium are:
\(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{OH}^-(\mathrm{aq})\)
and \(6\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 3\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 6\mathrm{e}^-\).
Adding these yields the balanced equation:
\(2\mathrm{MnO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 6\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 3\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{OH}^-(\mathrm{aq})\).
This contains \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The stoichiometric coefficients and positions of water are:
• Oxidation of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) by \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) in acid has \(7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side.
• Oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\) by \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) in acid has \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the product side.
• Oxidation of \(\mathrm{Br}^-\) by \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) in base has \(1\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side.
• Oxidation of \(\mathrm{I}^-\) by \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) in base has \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) on the reactant side.
The correct combination is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q07 - Indicators and observation in redox titration methods

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the indicator principles and visual observations in redox titrations:

List-I (Titration / Reaction System) List-II (Indicator Mechanism / Visual End Point)
A. Permanganate titration against \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) or \(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{O}_4^{2-}\) I. Starch indicator gives an intense blue colour that disappears once iodine is fully consumed
B. Dichromate titration against \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) in acidic medium II. Reagent acts as self-indicator; first lasting pink tinge appears at equivalence point
C. Iodometric titration of liberated \(\mathrm{I}_2\) with \(\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-}\) III. Diphenylamine is oxidised just after equivalence point to produce an intense blue colour
D. Reaction of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions with excess iodide ions IV. Iodine is liberated quantitatively along with the formation of cuprous iodide (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2\)) precipitate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Permanganate as a self-indicator
In permanganate titrations, \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) is intensely coloured. Once the reducing agent (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) or oxalate) is completely oxidized, the very first excess drop of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) imparts a lasting pale pink colour at concentrations as low as \(10^{-6}\mathrm{\ mol\ dm}^{-3}\). Hence, it acts as a self-indicator.

Step 2: Dichromate indicator mechanism
Potassium dichromate (\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\)) is not a self-indicator because its reduction product \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) is green, masking subtle colour shifts. It requires an external redox-sensitive indicator such as diphenylamine, which is oxidized by the first slight excess of dichromate immediately after the equivalence point to produce an intense blue colour.

Step 3: Iodometric titration with thiosulfate
In titrations involving free iodine and sodium thiosulfate (\(\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-}\)), starch is added as a specific indicator. Starch forms an intense deep-blue adsorption complex with molecular iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_3^-\)). At the end point, the reduction of iodine to iodide causes the sudden and complete disappearance of the blue colour.

Step 4: Oxidation of iodide by cupric ions
When copper(II) ions react with excess iodide ions, copper(II) is reduced to copper(I), precipitating insoluble white cuprous iodide (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2\)), while iodide is oxidised to molecular iodine via the reaction:
\(2\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{aq})\).
The liberated iodine can subsequently be titrated against standard thiosulfate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct indicator correspondences are:
• Permanganate titration corresponds to self-indicator action with a lasting pink tinge.
• Dichromate titration corresponds to diphenylamine producing an intense blue colour at the end point.
• Iodometric titration corresponds to starch giving an intense blue colour that disappears when iodine is reduced.
• Reaction of copper(II) with iodide corresponds to formation of \(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2\) precipitate and liberation of \(\mathrm{I}_2\).
The correct combination is A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q08 - Disproportionation behavior of chlorine oxoanions species

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II to correlate the oxoanions of chlorine with their characteristic disproportionation pathways:

List-I (Chlorine Oxoanion) List-II (Disproportionation Characteristics)
A. \(\mathrm{ClO}^-\) I. Disproportionates to yield \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) and \(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\)
B. \(\mathrm{ClO}_2^-\) II. Does not disproportionate because chlorine is in its maximum group oxidation state (\(+7\))
C. \(\mathrm{ClO}_3^-\) III. Disproportionates to yield \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) and \(\mathrm{ClO}_3^-\)
D. \(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\) IV. Photochemically disproportionates to yield \(\mathrm{ClO}_3^-\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Disproportionation of hypochlorite ion
In the hypochlorite ion (\(\mathrm{ClO}^-\)), chlorine is in the \(+1\) oxidation state. It readily disproportionates according to the reaction:
\(3\mathrm{ClO}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{ClO}_3^-\).
Chlorine experiences both reduction to \(-1\) in chloride and oxidation to \(+5\) in chlorate.

Step 2: Disproportionation of chlorite ion
In the chlorite ion (\(\mathrm{ClO}_2^-\)), chlorine exhibits an oxidation state of \(+3\). Under photochemical excitation (\(h\nu\)), it disproportionates as:
\(6\mathrm{ClO}_2^- \xrightarrow{h\nu} 4\mathrm{ClO}_3^- + 2\mathrm{Cl}^-\).
Chlorine increases its oxidation state from \(+3\) to \(+5\) in chlorate and decreases to \(-1\) in chloride.

Step 3: Disproportionation of chlorate ion
In the chlorate ion (\(\mathrm{ClO}_3^-\)), chlorine exhibits an oxidation state of \(+5\). Upon heating or disproportionation, it follows the reaction:
\(4\mathrm{ClO}_3^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}^- + 3\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).
Chlorine decreases its oxidation state from \(+5\) to \(-1\) in chloride and increases to \(+7\) in perchlorate.

Step 4: Non-disproportionation of perchlorate ion
In the perchlorate ion (\(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\)), chlorine is in its highest possible group oxidation state of \(+7\) (since group number is 17, maximum oxidation state is \(17 - 10 = +7\)). For an element to undergo disproportionation, it must exist in an intermediate oxidation state and be capable of forming both higher and lower oxidation states. Because chlorine cannot increase its oxidation number beyond \(+7\), perchlorate cannot disproportionate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The behavior of the chlorine oxoanions matches as follows:
• Hypochlorite disproportionates to yield chloride and chlorate.
• Chlorite photochemically disproportionates to yield chlorate and chloride.
• Chlorate disproportionates to yield chloride and perchlorate.
• Perchlorate does not disproportionate because chlorine is in its maximum oxidation state of \(+7\).
The correct combination is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q09 - Structural oxidation states of fractional paradox species

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II to correlate compounds displaying fractional average oxidation numbers with their actual constituent structural oxidation states:

List-I (Chemical Compound) List-II (Individual Structural Oxidation States)
A. Carbon suboxide (\(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{O}_2\)) I. Two terminal atoms each at \(+6\) and one central atom at \(+4\)
B. Tribromooctaoxide (\(\mathrm{Br}_3\mathrm{O}_8\)) II. Stoichiometric mixed oxide composed of one metal ion at \(+2\) and two metal ions at \(+3\)
C. Tetrathionate ion (\(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\)) III. Two terminal atoms each at \(+2\) and one central atom at \(0\)
D. Ferrosoferric oxide (\(\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{O}_4\)) IV. Two terminal atoms each at \(+5\) and two central atoms each at \(0\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural oxidation states in carbon suboxide
The Lewis structure of carbon suboxide is \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}^*=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\). Each of the two terminal carbon atoms is bonded to a more electronegative oxygen atom via a double bond and to a carbon atom via a double bond, giving them each an oxidation state of \(+2\). The central carbon atom is bonded exclusively to two identical carbon atoms, giving it an oxidation state of \(0\). The average is \(\frac{+2 + 0 + 2}{3} = +\frac{4}{3}\).

Step 2: Structural oxidation states in tribromooctaoxide
In \(\mathrm{Br}_3\mathrm{O}_8\), the structure has three linearly linked bromine atoms: \(\mathrm{O}_3\mathrm{Br}-\mathrm{BrO}_2-\mathrm{BrO}_3\). Each of the two terminal bromine atoms is bonded to three oxygen atoms, which assigns them an oxidation state of \(+6\) each. The central bromine atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms and two bromine atoms, giving it an oxidation state of \(+4\). The average is \(\frac{+6 + 4 + 6}{3} = +\frac{16}{3}\).

Step 3: Structural oxidation states in tetrathionate ion
In \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\), the structure consists of a sulfur chain: \([^{-}O_3\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{S}^*-\mathrm{S}^*-\mathrm{SO}_3^-]\). The two terminal sulfur atoms are bonded to three oxygen atoms each, placing them in the \(+5\) oxidation state. The two central sulfur atoms participate only in homonuclear sulfur-sulfur bonds, giving each of them an oxidation state of \(0\). The average is \(\frac{+5 + 0 + 0 + 5}{4} = +2.5\).

Step 4: Stoichiometric composition of ferrosoferric oxide
The mixed oxide \(\mathrm{Fe}_3\mathrm{O}_4\) has an apparent fractional average oxidation state of \(+\frac{8}{3}\). In reality, it is a stoichiometric mixed crystal composed of one mole of ferrous oxide (\(\mathrm{FeO}\)) and one mole of ferric oxide (\(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)). Consequently, one iron atom is present as \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) (oxidation state \(+2\)) and two iron atoms are present as \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) (oxidation state \(+3\)).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The structural assignments correspond as follows:
• Carbon suboxide consists of two terminal atoms at \(+2\) and one central atom at \(0\).
• Tribromooctaoxide consists of two terminal atoms at \(+6\) and one central atom at \(+4\).
• Tetrathionate ion consists of two terminal atoms at \(+5\) and two central atoms at \(0\).
• Ferrosoferric oxide consists of one iron atom at \(+2\) and two iron atoms at \(+3\).
The correct combination is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q10 - Standard reduction potentials and feasibility of reactions

questiontext.text:
Given standard reduction potentials at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\):
\(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{F}_2/\mathrm{F}^-) = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag}) = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}/\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77\mathrm{\ V}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{I}_2/\mathrm{I}^-) = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}) = +0.34\mathrm{\ V}\), and \(\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}) = -0.76\mathrm{\ V}\).
Match List-I with List-II regarding the electrochemical characteristics and thermodynamic feasibility of the processes:

List-I (Redox System / Process) List-II (Potential and Feasibility at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\))
A. Reaction between \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})\) and \(\mathrm{I}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})\) I. Non-feasible because standard cell potential is negative (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -0.03\mathrm{\ V}\))
B. Reaction between \(\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})\) and \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq})\) II. Feasible and spontaneous because \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.23\mathrm{\ V} > 0\)
C. Reaction between \(\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s})\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})\) in Daniell cell III. Possesses the highest positive reduction potential (\(+2.87\mathrm{\ V}\)), making it the strongest oxidant
D. Half-reaction: \(\mathrm{F}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{F}^-(\mathrm{aq})\) IV. Highly spontaneous reaction with standard cell potential \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +1.10\mathrm{\ V}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Feasibility of reaction between ferric ion and iodide
The proposed reaction is \(2\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s})\).
Cathode (reduction): \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.77\mathrm{\ V}\).
Anode (oxidation): \(2\mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\).
\(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = \mathrm{E}^\circ(\text{cathode}) - \mathrm{E}^\circ(\text{anode}) = +0.77\mathrm{\ V} - 0.54\mathrm{\ V} = +0.23\mathrm{\ V}\).
Because \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\), \(\Delta G^\circ = -nF\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} < 0\), the reaction is spontaneous and feasible under standard conditions.

Step 2: Feasibility of reaction between metallic silver and ferric ion
The proposed reaction is \(\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})\).
Cathode (reduction): \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.77\mathrm{\ V}\).
Anode (oxidation): \(\mathrm{Ag} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^+ + \mathrm{e}^-\), \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}\).
\(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.77\mathrm{\ V} - 0.80\mathrm{\ V} = -0.03\mathrm{\ V}\).
Because \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} < 0\), the reaction cannot proceed spontaneously under standard conditions.

Step 3: Daniell cell reaction
For the reaction \(\mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{s})\):
Cathode (reduction of copper): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.34\mathrm{\ V}\).
Anode (oxidation of zinc): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = -0.76\mathrm{\ V}\).
\(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.34\mathrm{\ V} - (-0.76\mathrm{\ V}) = +1.10\mathrm{\ V}\).
This represents a highly spontaneous galvanic cell reaction.

Step 4: Oxidising capability of elemental fluorine
The standard electrode potential of the \(\mathrm{F}_2/\mathrm{F}^-\) couple is \(+2.87\mathrm{\ V}\), which is the highest positive value in the electrochemical series. A higher positive reduction potential indicates a maximum tendency of the oxidised form to accept electrons and be reduced, making \(\mathrm{F}_2\) the strongest oxidising agent listed.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The electrochemical features match as follows:
• Reaction of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) with \(\mathrm{I}^-\) is feasible with \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.23\mathrm{\ V}\).
• Reaction of \(\mathrm{Ag}\) with \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) is non-feasible with \(\mathrm{E}^\circ_{\text{cell}} = -0.03\mathrm{\ V}\).
• Daniell cell reaction produces a cell potential of \(+1.10\mathrm{\ V}\).
• Reduction of \(\mathrm{F}_2\) possesses \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}\), acting as the strongest oxidizing couple.
The correct combination is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q01 - Oxidation number of phosphorus in sodium dihydrogen phosphate

questiontext.text: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in sodium dihydrogen phosphate, \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Compound: \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\). The compound is neutral, so the sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in the formula unit is zero.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Sodium is an alkali metal with an oxidation number of \(+1\). Hydrogen combined with non-metals has an oxidation number of \(+1\). Oxygen typically has an oxidation number of \(-2\). Let the oxidation number of phosphorus be \(x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound equals zero:
\[1 \times (\text{O.N. of Na}) + 2 \times (\text{O.N. of H}) + 1 \times (\text{O.N. of P}) + 4 \times (\text{O.N. of O}) = 0\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values into the equation:
\[1(+1) + 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\]
\[1 + 2 + x - 8 = 0\]
\[x + 3 - 8 = 0\]
\[x - 5 = 0 \implies x = +5\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying: \(+1 + 2(+1) + 5 + 4(-2) = 1 + 2 + 5 - 8 = 0\). The oxidation number of phosphorus in \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\) is \(+5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q02 - Oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate

questiontext.text: Calculate the oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate, \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The chemical formula is \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\). The overall charge on the formula unit is zero.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Potassium is an alkali metal, so its oxidation number is \(+1\). Oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\). Let \(x\) represent the oxidation number of manganese.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral molecule must equal zero:
\[2 \times (\text{O.N. of K}) + 1 \times (\text{O.N. of Mn}) + 4 \times (\text{O.N. of O}) = 0\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the oxidation numbers into the summation equation:
\[2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\]
\[+2 + x - 8 = 0\]
\[x - 6 = 0 \implies x = +6\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking: \(2(+1) + 6 + 4(-2) = 2 + 6 - 8 = 0\). The oxidation number of manganese in \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) is \(+6\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q03 - Oxidation number of boron in sodium borohydride

questiontext.text: Determine the oxidation number of boron in sodium borohydride, \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given compound is \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\), which is an ionic compound consisting of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and the borohydride anion \(\mathrm{BH_4^-}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Sodium is assigned an oxidation state of \(+1\). In metal hydrides and complex hydrides with less electronegative elements (electronegativity of \(\mathrm{H} = 2.1\), \(\mathrm{B} = 2.0\)), hydrogen is present as hydride with an oxidation state of \(-1\). Let the oxidation number of boron be \(x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For the neutral compound \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\):
\[(\text{O.N. of Na}) + (\text{O.N. of B}) + 4 \times (\text{O.N. of H}) = 0\]
Equivalently, for the anion \(\mathrm{BH_4^-}\), the sum of oxidation numbers equals \(-1\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Using the neutral formula:
\[1(+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0\]
\[1 + x - 4 = 0\]
\[x - 3 = 0 \implies x = +3\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Evaluating: \(+1 + (+3) + 4(-1) = 4 - 4 = 0\). The oxidation number of boron is \(+3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q04 - Oxidation state of sulphur in pyrosulphuric acid

questiontext.text: What is the oxidation state of sulphur in pyrosulphuric acid (oleum), \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Formula: \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\). Overall molecular charge is \(0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Hydrogen has an oxidation state of \(+1\). Oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\). Let the oxidation state of each sulphur atom be \(x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In a neutral molecule, the sum of all oxidation states is zero:
\[2 \times (\text{O.N. of H}) + 2 \times (\text{O.N. of S}) + 7 \times (\text{O.N. of O}) = 0\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the assigned values:
\[2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0\]
\[2 + 2x - 14 = 0\]
\[2x - 12 = 0 \implies 2x = 12 \implies x = +6\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking: \(2(1) + 2(6) + 7(-2) = 2 + 12 - 14 = 0\). The oxidation state of sulphur is \(+6\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q05 - Change in oxidation state of iron in potassium ferrocyanide oxidation

questiontext.text:
In the oxidation reaction:
\[2\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]} + \mathrm{H_2O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]} + 2\mathrm{KOH}\]
what is the change in the oxidation state of the iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\)) atom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reactant complex: \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\).
Product complex: \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\).
The cyanide ligand (\(\mathrm{CN^-}\)) has a formal charge and oxidation state of \(-1\). Potassium ion (\(\mathrm{K^+}\)) is \(+1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(x_1\) be the oxidation state of iron in \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) and \(x_2\) be the oxidation state of iron in \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\):
\[4(+1) + x_1 + 6(-1) = 0 \implies x_1 - 2 = 0 \implies x_1 = +2\]
In \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\):
\[3(+1) + x_2 + 6(-1) = 0 \implies x_2 - 3 = 0 \implies x_2 = +3\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The magnitude of the change in oxidation state of iron is:
\[\Delta \text{O.N.} = x_2 - x_1 = (+3) - (+2) = +1\]
Thus, the oxidation state increases by \(1\) unit (from \(+2\) to \(+3\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The iron is oxidized from ferrous (\(+2\)) to ferric (\(+3\)), representing a change of \(+1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q06 - Difference in average oxidation state of sulphur between tetrathionate and thiosulphate

questiontext.text: In iodometric titrations, thiosulphate ion (\(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\)) is oxidized to tetrathionate ion (\(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\)). What is the difference between the average oxidation state of sulphur in \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\) and in \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial species: thiosulphate ion, \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\).
Final species: tetrathionate ion, \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\).
Oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(x_1\) be the average oxidation state of sulphur in \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\) and \(x_2\) be the average oxidation state of sulphur in \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Sum of oxidation numbers equals the net ionic charge:
For \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\): \(2x_1 + 3(-2) = -2\)
For \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\): \(4x_2 + 6(-2) = -2\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(x_1\):
\[2x_1 - 6 = -2 \implies 2x_1 = +4 \implies x_1 = +2.0\]
Calculate \(x_2\):
\[4x_2 - 12 = -2 \implies 4x_2 = +10 \implies x_2 = +\frac{10}{4} = +2.5\]
Find the difference \((x_2 - x_1)\):
\[\Delta x = +2.5 - (+2.0) = +0.5\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The average oxidation state increases from \(+2.0\) to \(+2.5\), giving an increase of \(+0.5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q07 - Fractional oxidation state and individual oxidation states in tribromooctaoxide

questiontext.text: In tribromooctaoxide (\(\mathrm{Br_3O_8}\)), what are the individual oxidation states of the terminal bromine atoms and the central bromine atom, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Compound: \(\mathrm{Br_3O_8}\).
Structure: The three bromine atoms form a linear chain \(\mathrm{O_3Br - Br(O_2) - BrO_3}\), in which each of the two terminal bromine atoms is bonded to three oxygen atoms and the central bromine atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxygen has higher electronegativity than bromine, taking an oxidation number of \(-2\). Bromine-bromine bonds between identical atoms contribute \(0\) to the oxidation state.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For each terminal \(\mathrm{Br}\) bonded to \(3\) oxygen atoms: \(\text{O.N.} = 3 \times (+2) = +6\).
For the central \(\mathrm{Br}\) bonded to \(2\) oxygen atoms: \(\text{O.N.} = 2 \times (+2) = +4\).
Average oxidation number: \(\frac{2(+6) + 1(+4)}{3} = \frac{16}{3}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Terminal bromine atoms each have an oxidation state of \(+6\).
The central bromine atom has an oxidation state of \(+4\).
Thus, the individual oxidation states are \(+6\) for the terminal atoms and \(+4\) for the central atom.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total sum of oxidation numbers: \(2(+6) + 1(+4) + 8(-2) = 12 + 4 - 16 = 0\), satisfying molecular neutrality. The respective oxidation states are \(+6\) and \(+4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q08 - Difference in average oxidation number of carbon between ethanol and acetic acid

questiontext.text: Calculate the change in the average oxidation number of carbon when ethanol (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)) is completely oxidized to acetic acid (\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reactant: Ethanol, molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\).
Product: Acetic acid, molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Hydrogen is assigned \(+1\); oxygen is assigned \(-2\). Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) be the average oxidation numbers of carbon in ethanol and acetic acid, respectively.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\): \(2x_1 + 6(+1) + 1(-2) = 0\)
For \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\): \(2x_2 + 4(+1) + 2(-2) = 0\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\):
\[2x_1 + 6 - 2 = 0 \implies 2x_1 + 4 = 0 \implies 2x_1 = -4 \implies x_1 = -2\]
For \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}\):
\[2x_2 + 4 - 4 = 0 \implies 2x_2 = 0 \implies x_2 = 0\]
Change in average oxidation number:
\[\Delta x = x_2 - x_1 = 0 - (-2) = +2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The average oxidation state of carbon changes from \(-2\) in ethanol to \(0\) in acetic acid, representing an increase of \(2\) units.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q09 - Number of electrons transferred per mole of dichromate in acidic sulphite oxidation

questiontext.text:
In acidic solution, dichromate ion oxidizes sulphite ion according to the balanced equation:
\[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\]
How many moles of electrons are transferred per mole of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) reduced?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Balanced equation: \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\).
The reactant contains \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxidation number of \(\mathrm{Cr}\) in \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\):
\[2x + 7(-2) = -2 \implies 2x = 12 \implies x = +6\]
Oxidation number of \(\mathrm{Cr}\) in \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(+3\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The reduction half-reaction is:
\[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Each chromium atom undergoes a change from \(+6\) to \(+3\), requiring \(3\text{ e^-}\).
Since each dichromate ion contains \(2\) chromium atoms, total electrons accepted per dichromate ion:
\[n = 2 \times (6 - 3) = 6\text{ moles of electrons}\]
Alternatively, for the oxidation half-reaction: \(3\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{e^-}\), confirming \(6\text{ moles of electrons}\) are transferred.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The net charge and electrons are conserved at \(6\text{ moles of electrons}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q10 - Moles of iodine produced per mole of permanganate in acidic medium

questiontext.text: In acidic solution, permanganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)) oxidizes iodide ion (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) to iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\)). How many moles of \(\mathrm{I_2}\) are produced per mole of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) consumed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Permanganate ion in acidic medium reduces to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\). Iodide ion (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) is oxidized to molecular iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\).
Oxidation half-reaction: \(2\mathrm{I^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equating electrons gained and lost:
Multiply the reduction half-reaction by \(2\) and the oxidation half-reaction by \(5\):
\[2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} + 10\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}\]
\[10\mathrm{I^-} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{I_2} + 10\mathrm{e^-}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Adding the two half-reactions gives the overall balanced equation:
\[2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 10\mathrm{I^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{I_2} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}\]
From the stoichiometry, \(2\text{ moles of } \mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) produce \(5\text{ moles of } \mathrm{I_2}\).
Therefore, \(1\text{ mole of } \mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) produces:
\[\text{Moles of } \mathrm{I_2} = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5\text{ mol}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking by electron balance: \(1\text{ mol of } \mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) accepts \(5\text{ mol of e^-}\). Each mole of \(\mathrm{I_2}\) formed releases \(2\text{ mol of e^-}\). Thus, \(\frac{5}{2} = 2.5\text{ mol of } \mathrm{I_2}\) are formed.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q11 - Stoichiometric coefficient sum in acidic permanganate iron titration

questiontext.text:
When the following redox reaction is balanced in an acidic medium using the smallest integer coefficients:
\[a\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + b\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + c\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow d\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + e\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + f\mathrm{H_2O}\]
what is the sum of all stoichiometric coefficients, \((a + b + c + d + e + f)\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Unbalanced equation: \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Acidic medium. The oxidation number of \(\mathrm{Mn}\) changes from \(+7\) to \(+2\) (decrease of \(5\)). The oxidation number of \(\mathrm{Fe}\) changes from \(+2\) to \(+3\) (increase of \(1\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Half-reaction method:
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + \mathrm{e^-}\)
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Multiply the oxidation half-reaction by \(5\) to equalize electrons transferred:
\[5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 5\mathrm{e^-}\]
Combine with the reduction half-reaction:
\[1\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 1\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\]
Identifying the coefficients:
\[a = 1,\quad b = 5,\quad c = 8,\quad d = 1,\quad e = 5,\quad f = 4\]
Sum of coefficients:
\[a + b + c + d + e + f = 1 + 5 + 8 + 1 + 5 + 4 = 24\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying atoms and charges: LHS charge \(= -1 + 5(+2) + 8(+1) = +17\); RHS charge \(= +2 + 5(+3) = +17\). Atoms: \(1\text{ Mn}\), \(5\text{ Fe}\), \(8\text{ H}\), \(4\text{ O}\) on both sides. The sum is \(24\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q12 - Ratio of hydroxide ions to water molecules in basic permanganate bromide oxidation

questiontext.text: In a basic aqueous medium, permanganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)) oxidizes bromide ion (\(\mathrm{Br^-}\)) to bromate ion (\(\mathrm{BrO_3^-}\)) while being reduced to manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\)). When balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the stoichiometric ratio of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reactants: \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\), \(\mathrm{Br^-}\). Products: \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\), \(\mathrm{BrO_3^-}\). Medium: Basic aqueous.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Mn}\) changes from \(+7\) to \(+4\) (gains \(3\text{ e^-}\)).
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Br}\) changes from \(-1\) to \(+5\) (loses \(6\text{ e^-}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reduction half-reaction in base:
\[\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} + 3\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{OH^-}\]
Oxidation half-reaction in base:
\[\mathrm{Br^-} + 6\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{BrO_3^-} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} + 6\mathrm{e^-}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Multiply the reduction half-reaction by \(2\) to equalize electrons (\(6\text{ e^-}\)):
\[2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} + 6\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 8\mathrm{OH^-}\]
Add the oxidation half-reaction:
\[2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Br^-} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} + 6\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{BrO_3^-} + 8\mathrm{OH^-} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\]
Cancel common species on both sides (\(3\mathrm{H_2O}\) and \(6\mathrm{OH^-}\)):
\[2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Br^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{BrO_3^-} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\]
The stoichiometric coefficient of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) is \(2\) and that of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is \(1\).
The ratio of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is \(\frac{2}{1} = 2:1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Charge check: LHS \(= 2(-1) + (-1) = -3\); RHS \(= -1 + 2(-1) = -3\). Atoms check: \(2\text{ Mn}\), \(9\text{ O}\), \(2\text{ H}\), \(1\text{ Br}\) on both sides. The ratio is \(2:1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q13 - Standard cell potential of the Daniell cell

questiontext.text:
The standard reduction potentials for zinc and copper electrodes are given as:
\[E^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\]
\[E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]
What is the standard cell potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) of the Daniell cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a galvanic cell (Daniell cell), the cathode is the electrode with the more positive standard reduction potential where reduction occurs. Copper acts as the cathode, and zinc acts as the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The standard electromotive force of the cell is given by:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the standard reduction potentials:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = (+0.34\text{ V}) - (-0.76\text{ V})\]
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.34\text{ V} + 0.76\text{ V} = +1.10\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\) (\(+1.10\text{ V}\)), the spontaneous cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\). The standard potential is \(+1.10\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q14 - Standard EMF of zinc silver electrochemical cell

questiontext.text:
An electrochemical cell is constructed from standard zinc and silver half-cells:
\[\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} \parallel \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \mid \mathrm{Ag(s)}\]
Given that \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\) and \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\), what is the standard electromotive force (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Anode (oxidation half-cell): \(\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}\), \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}\).
Cathode (reduction half-cell): \(\mathrm{Ag^+ + e^- \rightarrow Ag}\), \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The standard cell potential is computed using reduction potentials according to IUPAC convention: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = (+0.80\text{ V}) - (-0.76\text{ V})\]
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.80\text{ V} + 0.76\text{ V} = +1.56\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The potential is positive (\(+1.56\text{ V}\)), confirming that silver ion reduction by metallic zinc is thermodynamically spontaneous under standard conditions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q15 - Maximum moles of nitric oxide produced from ammonia and dioxygen

questiontext.text:
Ammonia is catalytically oxidized to nitric oxide via the redox reaction:
\[4\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + 5\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\]
If a reaction vessel is charged with \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\), what is the maximum number of moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) that can be produced?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Balanced equation: \(4\mathrm{NH_3} + 5\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}\).
Initial quantities: \(n(\mathrm{NH_3}) = 2.0\text{ mol}\), \(n(\mathrm{O_2}) = 2.0\text{ mol}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The reaction proceeds to completion until the limiting reagent is exhausted.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Determine the stoichiometric ratio \(\frac{n}{\text{coefficient}}\):
For \(\mathrm{NH_3}\): \(\frac{2.0}{4} = 0.50\text{ mol of reaction runs}\)
For \(\mathrm{O_2}\): \(\frac{2.0}{5} = 0.40\text{ mol of reaction runs}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(0.40 < 0.50\), \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is the limiting reagent.
From the balanced reaction, \(5\text{ moles of } \mathrm{O_2}\) yield \(4\text{ moles of } \mathrm{NO}\).
Therefore, the maximum moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) produced are:
\[n(\mathrm{NO}) = 2.0\text{ mol } \mathrm{O_2} \times \left(\frac{4\text{ mol } \mathrm{NO}}{5\text{ mol } \mathrm{O_2}}\right) = \frac{8.0}{5} = 1.6\text{ mol}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Amount of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) consumed \(= 1.6\text{ mol}\), leaving \(0.4\text{ mol}\) unreacted. All \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) are consumed. The maximum yield of \(\mathrm{NO}\) is \(1.6\text{ mol}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q16 - Stoichiometry of hydrogen ions consumed in manganese three disproportionation

questiontext.text: In acidic aqueous solution, \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) ion is unstable and disproportionates into \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) and solid manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\)). How many moles of \(\mathrm{H^+}\) are consumed or produced when \(6.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) undergoes complete disproportionation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reactant: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}(aq)}\). Disproportionation products: \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{MnO_2(s)}\). Quantity: \(6.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) (\(+3\)) is oxidized to \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) (\(+4\)).
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) (\(+3\)) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(+2\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Writing and balancing half-reactions:
Oxidation: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{e^-}\)
Reduction: \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}} + \mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Add the two half-reactions:
\[2\mathrm{Mn^{3+}} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+}\]
This shows that for every \(2\text{ moles of } \mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) disproportionated, \(4\text{ moles of } \mathrm{H^+}\) are produced.
For \(6.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\):
\[n(\mathrm{H^+}) = 6.0\text{ mol } \mathrm{Mn^{3+}} \times \left(\frac{4\text{ mol } \mathrm{H^+}}{2\text{ mol } \mathrm{Mn^{3+}}}\right) = 12.0\text{ mol of } \mathrm{H^+} \text{ produced}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Charges for \(2\mathrm{Mn^{3+}} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+}\): LHS \(= 2(+3) = +6\); RHS \(= +2 + 0 + 4(+1) = +6\). Therefore, \(12\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H^+}\) are produced.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q17 - Ratio of electrons transferred in thiosulphate oxidation by bromine versus iodine

questiontext.text: Thiosulphate ion (\(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\)) reacts with bromine water to form sulphate ion (\(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)), whereas it reacts with iodine to form tetrathionate ion (\(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\)). What is the ratio of the number of moles of electrons lost per mole of \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\) in the reaction with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) to that in the reaction with \(\mathrm{I_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction 1 (with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\)): \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).
Reaction 2 (with \(\mathrm{I_2}\)): \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxidation numbers of sulphur:
In \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\): \(+2\).
In \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\): \(+6\).
In \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}}\): \(+2.5\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Change in oxidation number determines the number of electrons lost per sulphur atom, and multiplying by the number of sulphur atoms gives total electrons lost per formula unit.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In Reaction 1 (oxidation to sulphate):
Each sulphur atom goes from \(+2\) to \(+6\), losing \(4\text{ e^-}\).
For \(2\) sulphur atoms in \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\):
\[n_1 = 2 \times (6 - 2) = 8\text{ moles of electrons lost per mole of } \mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\]
Balancing: \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} + 5\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 10\mathrm{H^+} + 8\mathrm{e^-}\).
In Reaction 2 (oxidation to tetrathionate):
\[2\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{S_4O_6^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\]
Per mole of \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\):
\[n_2 = \frac{2}{2} = 1\text{ mole of electrons lost}\]
Ratio of electrons lost:
\[\text{Ratio} = \frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{8}{1} = 8:1\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, resulting in an eight-fold increase in electron extraction per mole of thiosulphate. The ratio is \(8:1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q18 - Molarity of ferrous sulphate solution titrated by potassium permanganate

questiontext.text: A \(25.0\text{ mL}\) sample of an aqueous \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) solution requires \(20.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.020\text{ M}\) acidified \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) solution for complete oxidation. What is the molarity of the \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Volume of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) solution (\(V_1\)) \(= 20.0\text{ mL}\).
Molarity of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) solution (\(M_1\)) \(= 0.020\text{ M}\).
Volume of \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) solution (\(V_2\)) \(= 25.0\text{ mL}\).
Medium: Acidic.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Under acidic conditions, \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) reduces to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (gain of \(5\text{ e^-}\), valence factor \(n_1 = 5\)).
\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) oxidizes to \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) (loss of \(1\text{ e^-}\), valence factor \(n_2 = 1\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the law of chemical equivalents:
\[N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2 \implies (M_1 \times n_1) V_1 = (M_2 \times n_2) V_2\]
Equivalently, from stoichiometry: \(1\text{ mol } \mathrm{MnO_4^-} \equiv 5\text{ mol } \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate millimoles of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\):
\[\text{mmol}(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}) = M_1 \times V_1 = 0.020\text{ M} \times 20.0\text{ mL} = 0.40\text{ mmol}\]
Calculate millimoles of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\):
\[\text{mmol}(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}) = 5 \times 0.40\text{ mmol} = 2.0\text{ mmol}\]
Calculate molarity of \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\):
\[M_2 = \frac{\text{mmol}(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}})}{V_2} = \frac{2.0\text{ mmol}}{25.0\text{ mL}} = 0.080\text{ M}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking via normality: \(N_1 = 0.020 \times 5 = 0.10\text{ N}\).
\(N_2 = \frac{N_1 V_1}{V_2} = \frac{0.10 \times 20.0}{25.0} = 0.080\text{ N}\).
Since \(n_2 = 1\), \(M_2 = 0.080\text{ M}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q19 - Oxidation state of xenon and electron change in xenon hexafluoride hydrolysis

questiontext.text:
In the disproportionation reaction of xenon hexafluoride in basic solution:
\[2\mathrm{XeF_6(s)} + 16\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}(aq)} + \mathrm{Xe(g)} + 12\mathrm{F^-(aq)} + 8\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\]
what is the oxidation number of xenon in the perxenate ion \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\), and how many electrons are transferred between the xenon atoms per mole of \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: \(2\mathrm{XeF_6} + 16\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}} + \mathrm{Xe} + 12\mathrm{F^-} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}\).
Reactant: \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\). Products containing xenon: \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) and elemental \(\mathrm{Xe}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Fluorine has an oxidation state of \(-1\). Oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\). Elemental xenon has an oxidation state of \(0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\): \(x + 6(-1) = 0 \implies x = +6\).
In \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\): \(y + 6(-2) = -4 \implies y - 12 = -4 \implies y = +8\).
In \(\mathrm{Xe(g)}\): oxidation number \(= 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
One xenon atom is oxidized from \(+6\) (in \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\)) to \(+8\) (in \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\)), losing \(2\text{ electrons}\).
The second xenon atom is reduced from \(+6\) (in \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\)) to \(0\) (in \(\mathrm{Xe(g)}\)), gaining \(6\text{ electrons}\).
For stoichiometry: to balance electron transfer, \(3\text{ atoms of Xe(+6)}\) must be oxidized to produce \(3\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) (\(3 \times 2 = 6\text{ e^-}\) lost) for each \(1\text{ atom of Xe(+6)}\) reduced to \(\mathrm{Xe(0)}\) (\(6\text{ e^-}\) gained).
When \(1\text{ mole of } \mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) is formed from \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\), exactly \(2\text{ moles of electrons}\) are lost in its oxidation from \(+6\) to \(+8\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The oxidation number of xenon in \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) is \(+8\), and the oxidation process involves a loss of \(2\text{ moles of electrons}\) per mole of \(\mathrm{XeO_6^{4-}}\) formed.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_CH07_MCQ_Q20 - Standard cell potential of copper one disproportionation

questiontext.text:
The standard reduction potentials for copper species are:
\[E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu^+}} = +0.15\text{ V}\]
\[E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^+/Cu}} = +0.52\text{ V}\]
What is the standard cell potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) for the disproportionation of copper(I) ion in aqueous solution:
\[2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Disproportionation reaction: \(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\).
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Cu^+} + \mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\), with \(E^\circ_{\text{red}} = +0.52\text{ V}\).
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\mathrm{Cu^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + \mathrm{e^-}\), with \(E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu^+}} = +0.15\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The cathode corresponds to the reduction of \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
The anode corresponds to the oxidation of \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The standard electromotive force of the disproportionation reaction is:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^+/Cu}} - E^\circ_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu^+}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the standard reduction potentials:
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = (+0.52\text{ V}) - (+0.15\text{ V}) = +0.37\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.37\text{ V} > 0\), the standard Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) is negative, indicating that the disproportionation of copper(I) in aqueous solution is spontaneous. The standard cell potential is \(+0.37\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of steps in balancing redox reactions

questiontext.text:
In balancing a chemical equation for a redox process in an acidic aqueous solution using the oxidation number method, consider the following procedural steps:

(I) Balance the total ionic charges on both sides of the equation by adding \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions.
(II) Write the correct skeletal chemical formulas for all reactants and products.
(III) Balance hydrogen atoms by adding appropriate numbers of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules, then verify oxygen atom balance.
(IV) Assign oxidation numbers to all elements and identify the atoms undergoing change in oxidation state.
(V) Calculate the increase and decrease in oxidation number per atom and multiply by suitable integers to equalize the total increase and decrease.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of steps from beginning to end?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initial Skeletal Formulation
The oxidation number method begins by writing down the correct skeletal chemical formula for each reactant and product involved in the reaction.

Step 2: Assigning Oxidation Numbers and Identifying Changes
The next step requires assigning oxidation numbers to every element in the equation according to standard rules, identifying which species undergo oxidation (increase in oxidation number) and which undergo reduction (decrease in oxidation number).

Step 3: Equalizing Increase and Decrease in Oxidation Number
The increase in oxidation number per atom for the reductant and the decrease in oxidation number per atom for the oxidant are calculated. Appropriate integer stoichiometric coefficients are placed before the formulas so that the total increase in oxidation number exactly equals the total decrease.

Step 4: Balancing Charge in Acidic Medium
Because the reaction takes place in an acidic aqueous medium, \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions are added to the appropriate side of the equation so that the net ionic charges on the reactant side and product side become identical.

Step 5: Balancing Hydrogen and Oxygen Atoms
Finally, the number of hydrogen atoms is balanced by adding \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules to the deficient side, and the equation is checked to ensure that the number of oxygen atoms is equal on both sides.

Step 6: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence of operations is writing skeletal formulas, followed by assigning oxidation numbers, equalizing oxidation number changes, balancing ionic charges with hydrogen ions, and finally balancing hydrogen and oxygen with water molecules: (II) → (IV) → (V) → (I) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q02 - Conceptual evolution of the definition of oxidation

questiontext.text:
Consider the conceptual milestones in the historical and pedagogical development of the definition of 'oxidation' in chemistry:

(I) Electronic transfer concept: Oxidation is defined as the loss of electron(s) by any chemical species.
(II) Limited classical definition: Oxidation is defined strictly as the addition of oxygen to an element or a compound.
(III) Modern unified concept: Oxidation is viewed as an increase in the oxidation number or a decrease in electron density around an atom.
(IV) Broadened classical definition: Oxidation is expanded to include the removal of hydrogen or the removal of electropositive elements.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological and conceptual progression of the term 'oxidation'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Earliest Classical Definition
Originally, the term oxidation was coined strictly to describe the direct combination of atmospheric oxygen with elements or compounds, such as \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\).

Step 2: Extension to Hydrogen and Electropositive Elements
As knowledge expanded through reactions like the combustion of methane and the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide, chemists reinterpreted oxidation to include the removal of hydrogen as well as the removal of other electropositive elements (such as potassium from potassium ferrocyanide).

Step 3: Formulation of the Electron Transfer Model
Upon recognizing that ionic solids consist of discrete cations and anions formed through redox changes (such as \(2\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)), oxidation was fundamentally reformulated as the loss of one or more electrons by any interacting species.

Step 4: Generalized Oxidation Number and Electron Density Description
To track electron shifts in covalent molecules where formal electron transfer is incomplete, the concept of oxidation number was established. More recently, oxidation has been unified as an increase in oxidation state or a decrease in electron density around the atom.

Step 5: Final Answer
The sequential evolution proceeds from the limited classical definition of oxygen addition, to the broadened classical definition involving hydrogen removal, followed by the electronic transfer concept, and finally the generalized oxidation number and electron density concept: (II) → (IV) → (I) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q03 - Balancing reduction half-reaction in basic medium

questiontext.text:
When balancing the reduction half-reaction of permanganate ion to manganese dioxide in a basic aqueous solution using the half-reaction method:

\[\mathrm{MnO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2(\mathrm{s})\]

consider the following sequence of operations:

(I) Add \(4\mathrm{H}^+\) ions to the left side to balance hydrogen atoms.
(II) Add \(2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules to the right side to balance oxygen atoms.
(III) Add \(4\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions to both sides of the equation and combine \(\mathrm{H}^+\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) on the left side to form \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
(IV) Cancel duplicate water molecules to obtain \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).
(V) Add \(3\mathrm{e}^-\) to the left side to balance electrical charges.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Balancing Oxygen Atoms with Water
In the skeletal half-reaction \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2\), manganese is already balanced. The reactant side has 4 oxygen atoms and the product side has 2. Two water molecules must first be added to the product side:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Balancing Hydrogen Atoms with Hydrogen Ions
To balance the 4 hydrogen atoms introduced on the right side, \(4\mathrm{H}^+\) ions are added to the left side:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Conversion to Basic Medium
Because the reaction takes place in basic medium, for every \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion present, an equal number of \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions (\(4\mathrm{OH}^-\)) must be added to both sides of the equation. On the left side, \(4\mathrm{H}^+ + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\) combine to form \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\):
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 4: Simplifying Water Molecules
Cancelling two water molecules from both sides gives the simplified atom-balanced equation:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 5: Balancing Electric Charge with Electrons
The net charge on the left is \(-1\) and on the right is \(-4\). To balance charges, \(3\mathrm{e}^-\) must be added to the left side, yielding the fully balanced reduction half-reaction:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 6: Final Answer
The correct sequence of operations is balancing oxygen with water, balancing hydrogen with hydrogen ions, converting to basic medium by adding hydroxide ions, cancelling duplicate water molecules, and finally adding electrons to balance charge: (II) → (I) → (III) → (IV) → (V).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q04 - Chronological stages of competitive zinc copper reaction

questiontext.text:
In a laboratory experiment investigating competitive electron transfer, a clean strip of metallic zinc is placed into an aqueous solution of copper nitrate. Consider the following observations and operations:

(I) The intensity of the deep blue colour of the solution begins to diminish, and a reddish-brown crust starts depositing on the surface of the zinc rod.
(II) The clean zinc strip is placed into the deep blue copper nitrate solution.
(III) Addition of aqueous ammonia to make the solution alkaline followed by passing \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) gas produces a characteristic white precipitate.
(IV) The blue colour completely disappears leaving a colourless solution with metallic copper deposited on the zinc rod.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of experimental observations and procedures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Placement of Zinc in Solution
The experiment commences when a polished, clean strip of metallic zinc is immersed in a beaker filled with an aqueous copper nitrate solution, which has a characteristic deep blue colour due to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions.

Step 2: Progress of Electron Transfer and Color Fading
As electron transfer initiates, zinc atoms lose electrons to form \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions while copper ions gain electrons to form elemental copper. The intensity of the blue colour gradually fades as the concentration of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) decreases, and a reddish-brown layer of copper metal begins coating the zinc rod.

Step 3: Complete Consumption of Copper Ions
After approximately one hour, the blue colour completely disappears, leaving a water-clear, colourless solution containing \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions and an appreciable deposit of reddish metallic copper on the rod.

Step 4: Confirmatory Chemical Test for Product Ions
To verify the formation of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions in the colourless solution, aqueous ammonia is added to make the medium alkaline, followed by bubbling hydrogen sulfide gas (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)), which results in the immediate precipitation of white zinc sulfide (\(\mathrm{ZnS}\)).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence is immersing the zinc strip, observing the fading of blue colour with copper deposition, complete disappearance of blue colour, and chemical confirmation with alkaline hydrogen sulfide: (II) → (I) → (IV) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q05 - Ordering of halogens by increasing oxidizing power

questiontext.text:
Based on the halogen activity series and their standard electrode reduction potentials at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\):

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{F}_2/\mathrm{F}^-) = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}_2/\mathrm{Cl}^-) = +1.36\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Br}_2/\mathrm{Br}^-) = +1.09\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{I}_2/\mathrm{I}^-) = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of halogens arranged in strictly increasing order of their power as oxidising agents?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Oxidising Strength and Electrode Potential
The power of an element to act as an oxidising agent corresponds to its tendency to gain electrons and undergo reduction. A higher, more positive standard reduction potential (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ\)) indicates a greater driving force for reduction and hence a stronger oxidising ability.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
Listing the given standard electrode potentials for the reduction half-reactions \(\mathrm{X}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{X}^-\):
• For iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For bromine (\(\mathrm{Br}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +1.09\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +1.36\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}\)

Step 3: Verification with Halogen Displacement Behavior
Chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide from aqueous halides (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 2\mathrm{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{Br}_2\)). Bromine displaces iodide (\(\mathrm{Br}_2 + 2\mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Br}^- + \mathrm{I}_2\)). Fluorine is so reactive that it oxidises the oxygen of water directly. Thus, oxidising power decreases down group 17 from fluorine to iodine.

Step 4: Final Answer
Arranging in strictly increasing order of oxidising power gives iodine as the weakest oxidant and fluorine as the strongest oxidant: \(\mathrm{I}_2 < \mathrm{Br}_2 < \mathrm{Cl}_2 < \mathrm{F}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q06 - Ordering of metals by increasing reducing power

questiontext.text:
Given the standard electrode reduction potentials at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\):

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag}) = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg}) = +0.79\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr}) = -0.74\mathrm{\ V},\]

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}) = -2.37\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{K}^+/\mathrm{K}) = -2.93\mathrm{\ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these metals arranged in strictly increasing order of their reducing power?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Reducing Power and Reduction Potential
A reducing agent acts by donating electrons and is itself oxidised. A more negative standard reduction potential (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ\)) indicates that the redox couple has a higher tendency to lose electrons than the standard hydrogen electrode, making the elemental metal a stronger reducing agent. Conversely, a more positive reduction potential signifies a weaker reducing agent.

Step 2: Tabulating Potential Values
Sorting the given standard reduction potentials from most positive to most negative:
• \(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg} = +0.79\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr} = -0.74\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg} = -2.37\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{K}^+/\mathrm{K} = -2.93\mathrm{\ V}\)

Step 3: Establishing the Sequence of Reducing Power
Since reducing power increases as \(\mathrm{E}^\circ\) becomes more negative:
Silver has the most positive reduction potential (\(+0.80\mathrm{\ V}\)) and is the weakest reducing agent.
Mercury is next (\(+0.79\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Chromium is stronger (\(-0.74\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Magnesium is stronger still (\(-2.37\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Potassium has the most negative potential (\(-2.93\mathrm{\ V}\)) and is the strongest reducing agent.

Step 4: Final Answer
The metals arranged in increasing order of reducing power follow the sequence: \(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Hg} < \mathrm{Cr} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q07 - Arrangement of sulfur species by oxidation number

questiontext.text:
Consider the following sulfur-containing species:

(I) Hydrogen sulfide, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)
(II) Tetrathionate ion, \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\)
(III) Elemental rhombic sulfur, \(\mathrm{S}_8\)
(IV) Sulfite ion, \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\)
(V) Sulfate ion, \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\)

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these species arranged in strictly increasing order of the oxidation state (or average oxidation state) of sulfur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculation for Hydrogen Sulfide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\))
Hydrogen bonded to a non-metal exhibits an oxidation state of \(+1\).
\(2(+1) + x = 0 \implies x = -2\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) has an oxidation number of \(-2\).

Step 2: Calculation for Elemental Sulfur (\(\mathrm{S}_8\))
In elemental or uncombined homoatomic forms, each atom bears an oxidation number of zero. Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{S}_8\) has an oxidation number of \(0\).

Step 3: Calculation for Tetrathionate Ion (\(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\))
Oxygen is assigned an oxidation state of \(-2\). Equating the algebraic sum to the ion charge of \(-2\):
\(4x + 6(-2) = -2 \implies 4x - 12 = -2 \implies 4x = +10 \implies x = +2.5\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\) has an average oxidation number of \(+2.5\).

Step 4: Calculation for Sulfite Ion (\(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\))
Equating the sum to the net charge of \(-2\):
\(x + 3(-2) = -2 \implies x - 6 = -2 \implies x = +4\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\) has an oxidation number of \(+4\).

Step 5: Calculation for Sulfate Ion (\(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\))
Equating the sum to the net charge of \(-2\):
\(x + 4(-2) = -2 \implies x - 8 = -2 \implies x = +6\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\) has an oxidation number of \(+6\).

Step 6: Final Answer
Arranging in strictly increasing numerical order: \(-2 < 0 < +2.5 < +4 < +6\). The corresponding sequence of species is (I) → (III) → (II) → (IV) → (V).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q08 - Procedural stages in an iodometric redox titration

questiontext.text:
In the quantitative iodometric titration of cupric ions (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\)) using standard sodium thiosulfate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) and starch indicator, consider the following experimental stages:

(I) Freshly prepared starch indicator is introduced into the pale straw-yellow solution, forming an intense deep-blue starch-iodine adsorption complex.
(II) Standard sodium thiosulfate solution is run from the burette into the liberated iodine solution until the dark reddish-brown colour fades to a pale straw-yellow.
(III) An excess of potassium iodide is added to the aqueous copper(II) solution, precipitating white cuprous iodide (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2\)) and liberating molecular iodine.
(IV) Titration with standard thiosulfate is continued dropwise until the deep-blue colour completely discharges, signalling the stoichiometric end point.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of stages during this analytical procedure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Liberation of Iodine by Reaction with Iodide
The procedure begins by adding excess potassium iodide (\(\mathrm{KI}\)) to an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions. Cupric ions oxidise iodide according to the redox reaction:
\(2\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{aq})\).
This reaction precipitates cuprous iodide as a white solid and releases an equimolar quantity of iodine, imparting an intense reddish-brown colour to the suspension.

Step 2: Pre-titration of Liberated Iodine
The liberated iodine is titrated against standard sodium thiosulfate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)). The reaction is:
\(\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\).
Thiosulfate is added until the dark reddish-brown colour of iodine is reduced to a faint pale straw-yellow.

Step 3: Timely Addition of Starch Indicator
Starch is not added at the beginning because high concentrations of iodine can irreversibly coagulate or bind to starch. When the solution reaches the pale straw-yellow stage, starch solution is introduced, immediately producing an intense, dark blue colour due to the formation of the starch-triiodide complex.

Step 4: Final Titration to End Point
Thiosulfate addition is resumed drop by drop with vigorous swirling until the final trace of iodine is converted to iodide ions, resulting in the sharp and permanent disappearance of the blue colour at the equivalence point.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological order of stages is generation of molecular iodine, pre-titration to straw-yellow colour, addition of starch indicator, and final discharge of blue colour: (III) → (II) → (I) → (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Classical oxidation involving removal of electropositive potassium

questiontext.text:
Consider the classical redox reaction:

\[2\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6](aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O_2(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6](aq)} + 2\mathrm{KOH(aq)}\]

According to the classical concept of redox reactions, potassium ferrocyanide undergoes oxidation because of which of the following reasons?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In classical chemistry, oxidation was initially defined as the addition of oxygen or an electronegative element to a substance, or the removal of hydrogen or an electropositive element from a substance.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reaction
In the reaction, \(2\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) is transformed into \(2\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\). The number of electropositive potassium atoms associated with each hexacyanidoferrate entity decreases from 4 to 3 as potassium forms \(\mathrm{KOH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The removal of the electropositive element potassium from potassium ferrocyanide constitutes oxidation under the classical definition.
Therefore, the final answer is the removal of the electropositive element potassium.

answer.text: Addition of dihydrogen to the complex ion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Classical reduction in mercuric chloride reaction

questiontext.text:
In the chemical reaction:

\[2\mathrm{HgCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{SnCl_2(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2(s)} + \mathrm{SnCl_4(aq)}\]

Which statement correctly describes the classical reduction process taking place?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the broadened classical definition, reduction is defined as the removal of oxygen or an electronegative element from a substance, or the addition of hydrogen or an electropositive element to a substance.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reaction
In \(2\mathrm{HgCl_2} + \mathrm{SnCl_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2} + \mathrm{SnCl_4}\), mercuric chloride (\(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\)) is converted to mercurous chloride (\(\mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2}\)). The ratio of mercury to chlorine changes from \(1:2\) to \(2:2\) (or \(1:1\)), which represents an effective addition of the electropositive element mercury to mercuric chloride. Simultaneously, \(\mathrm{SnCl_2}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{SnCl_4}\) by the addition of the electronegative element chlorine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\) undergoes reduction via the addition of the electropositive element mercury.
Therefore, the final answer is that \(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\) is reduced due to the addition of electropositive mercury.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{SnCl_2}\) is reduced due to the removal of electronegative chlorine.
\(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\) is reduced due to the addition of electropositive mercury.
\(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\) is oxidised due to the removal of electropositive mercury.
\(\mathrm{SnCl_4}\) is reduced due to the addition of electronegative chlorine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Identification of oxidised and reduced species in hydrogen sulphide reaction

questiontext.text:
In the reaction:

\[\mathrm{H_2S(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl(g)} + \mathrm{S(s)}\]

Which species undergoes oxidation and which species undergoes reduction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxidation involves the removal of hydrogen, the addition of an electronegative element, or an increase in oxidation number. Reduction involves the addition of hydrogen, the removal of an electronegative element, or a decrease in oxidation number.

Step 2: Evaluation of Species
In \(\mathrm{H_2S}\), the oxidation state of sulphur is \(-2\), which increases to \(0\) in elemental \(\mathrm{S}\); alternatively, the electropositive hydrogen is removed from sulphur. Hence, \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) is oxidised. In \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), the oxidation state of chlorine is \(0\), which decreases to \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{HCl}\); alternatively, hydrogen is added to chlorine. Hence, \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is reduced.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H_2S}\) undergoes oxidation and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) undergoes reduction.
Therefore, the final answer is that \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) is oxidised and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is reduced.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Electron transfer half reaction in sodium hydride synthesis

questiontext.text:
Consider the reaction between metallic sodium and dihydrogen gas:

\[2\mathrm{Na(s)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaH(s)}\]

Which statement correctly describes the half-reaction and redox roles in this process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An oxidation half-reaction represents the loss of electrons, and the species losing electrons acts as the reducing agent. A reduction half-reaction represents the gain of electrons, and the species gaining electrons acts as the oxidising agent.

Step 2: Evaluation of Half-Reactions
Sodium hydride is an ionic compound represented as \(\mathrm{Na^+H^-(s)}\). The complete process splits into two half-reactions:
Oxidation half-reaction: \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\)
Reduction half-reaction: \(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H^-}\)
Sodium donates electrons to hydrogen, so sodium is oxidised and functions as the reducing agent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxidation half-reaction is \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\), with sodium acting as the reducing agent.
Therefore, the final answer is that the oxidation half-reaction is \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\), and sodium acts as the reducing agent.
