name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q06 - Match electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions with attacking electrophiles

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Electrophilic Substitution of Benzene) List II (Active Electrophile Involved)
(A) Nitration with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) (I) Chloronium ion (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\))
(B) Chlorination with \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) (II) Acylium ion (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}^+\mathrm{O}\))
(C) Friedel-Crafts acylation with acetyl chloride and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) (III) Nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\))
(D) Sulphonation with fuming sulphuric acid (oleum) (IV) Neutral sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_3\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrophile in aromatic nitration
In the nitration of benzene, concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a Brønsted acid and protonates nitric acid. Subsequent elimination of water generates the active electrophile, the nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\)):
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + \mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HSO}_4^- + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}^+-\mathrm{NO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NO}_2^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{HSO}_4^-\]

Step 2: Electrophile in aromatic halogenation
During chlorination, the Lewis acid catalyst anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)) polarizes and cleaves the chlorine molecule by accepting a chloride ion, generating the chloronium ion electrophile (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\)):
\[\mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}^+ + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\]

Step 3: Electrophile in Friedel-Crafts acylation
Reaction of an acyl halide such as acetyl chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride leads to abstraction of chloride by the Lewis acid to generate the resonance-stabilized acylium ion (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}^+=\mathrm{O} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{O}^+\)):
\[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCl} + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}^+\mathrm{O} + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\]

Step 4: Electrophile in sulphonation
Sulphonation is carried out using fuming sulphuric acid containing dissolved sulphur trioxide. In this medium, the strong electrophile is the neutral electrophilic molecule sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_3\)), in which the highly electronegative oxygen atoms render the central sulphur atom strongly electron-deficient.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The reactions matched with their respective electrophiles are: Nitration involves nitronium ion; Chlorination involves chloronium ion; Friedel-Crafts acylation involves acylium ion; and Sulphonation involves neutral sulphur trioxide.
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q07 - Match benzene ring substituents with directive and activating effects

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Substituent on Benzene Ring) List II (Electronic Nature and Directive Influence)
(A) \(-\mathrm{OH}\) (I) Strongly deactivating and meta-directing
(B) \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) (II) Strongly activating and ortho/para-directing
(C) \(-\mathrm{Cl}\) (III) Moderately deactivating and ortho/para-directing
(D) \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) (IV) Activating and ortho/para-directing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Directive effect and activation by the phenolic hydroxyl group
The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group exhibits a negative inductive effect (\(-I\)) but a much stronger positive resonance effect (\(+R\)) due to the delocalization of the oxygen lone pair into the ring. This greatly increases the electron density at the ortho- and para-positions relative to the meta-position, making the group strongly activating and ortho/para-directing.

Step 2: Directive effect and deactivation by the nitro group
The \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) group is strongly electron-withdrawing both by a powerful negative inductive effect (\(-I\)) and a strong negative resonance effect (\(-R\)). It reduces electron density throughout the ring, particularly at the ortho- and para-positions, rendering the ring strongly deactivated and directing electrophiles to the comparatively less electron-depleted meta-position.

Step 3: Anomalous effect of halogen substituents
In aryl halides such as chlorobenzene, chlorine has a strong electron-withdrawing inductive effect (\(-I\)) that outweighs its weak resonance electron donation (\(+R\)), decreasing the net electron density of the ring and making it moderately deactivating. However, resonance delocalization selectively places partial negative charges at the ortho- and para-positions, making halogens ortho/para-directing.

Step 4: Directive effect of an alkyl substituent
An alkyl group such as \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) donates electron density into the aromatic ring via inductive effect (\(+I\)) and hyperconjugation. This increases electron density preferentially at the ortho- and para-positions, rendering the methyl group activating and ortho/para-directing.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Matching each substituent with its behavior yields: The hydroxyl group is strongly activating and ortho/para-directing; The nitro group is strongly deactivating and meta-directing; The chloro group is moderately deactivating and ortho/para-directing; and The methyl group is activating and ortho/para-directing.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q08 - Match aromatic species with their pi electron counts

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II according to Hückel's rule of aromaticity (\((4n + 2)\pi\) electrons):

List I (Aromatic Species) List II (Hückel Integer \(n\) and \(\pi\)-Electron Count)
(A) Cyclopentadienyl anion (I) \(n = 2\) with \(10\pi\) electrons
(B) Cycloheptatrienyl cation (II) \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a five-membered ring
(C) Naphthalene (III) \(n = 3\) with \(14\pi\) electrons
(D) Anthracene (IV) \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a seven-membered ring

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Application of Hückel's rule to cyclopentadienyl anion
Cyclopentadienyl anion contains two conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds (\(4\pi\) electrons) and a non-bonding lone pair of electrons on the negatively charged carbon (\(2\pi\) electrons) fully delocalized over a planar 5-membered ring. The total number of \(\pi\) electrons is \(6\), satisfying the Hückel formula \(4n + 2 = 6\) with \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Application of Hückel's rule to cycloheptatrienyl cation
Cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion) has three conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds (\(6\pi\) electrons) and a vacant p-orbital on the positively charged carbon. The \(6\pi\) electrons are completely delocalized over the planar 7-membered ring, corresponding to \(4n + 2 = 6\) with \(n = 1\).

Step 3: Application of Hückel's rule to naphthalene
Naphthalene is a bicyclic aromatic hydrocarbon with two fused benzene rings. It has five conjugated double bonds providing a total of \(10\pi\) electrons fully delocalized across the planar framework, satisfying \(4n + 2 = 10\) with \(n = 2\).

Step 4: Application of Hückel's rule to anthracene
Anthracene is a tricyclic benzenoid hydrocarbon possessing three linearly fused benzene rings. It contains seven conjugated double bonds comprising \(14\pi\) electrons delocalized over the planar ring system, satisfying \(4n + 2 = 14\) with \(n = 3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Comparing the species with the electronic parameters: Cyclopentadienyl anion has \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a five-membered ring; Cycloheptatrienyl cation has \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a seven-membered ring; Naphthalene has \(n = 2\) with \(10\pi\) electrons; and Anthracene has \(n = 3\) with \(14\pi\) electrons.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q09 - Match alkenes with their respective ozonolysis cleavage products

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Alkene Subjected to Ozonolysis with \(\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) List II (Carbonyl Products Formed)
(A) But-2-ene (I) Propan-2-one and methanal
(B) 2-Methylprop-1-ene (II) Two moles of ethanal
(C) Propene (III) Ethanal and propanal
(D) Pent-2-ene (IV) Ethanal and methanal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cleavage of symmetrical but-2-ene
The structure of but-2-ene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\). Ozonolysis cleaves the carbon-carbon double bond, converting each \(=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\) fragment into an aldehyde molecule, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\). Hence, two moles of ethanal are produced.

Step 2: Cleavage of branched 2-methylprop-1-ene
The structure of 2-methylprop-1-ene is \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}_2\). Cleavage of the double bond transforms the disubstituted carbon fragment \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{C}=\) into a ketone, propan-2-one (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCH}_3\)), and the terminal \(=\mathrm{CH}_2\) fragment into an aldehyde, methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)).

Step 3: Cleavage of propene
The structure of propene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\). Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond into two carbonyl fragments: the \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\) portion becomes ethanal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)) and the \(=\mathrm{CH}_2\) portion becomes methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)).

Step 4: Cleavage of unsymmetrical pent-2-ene
The structure of pent-2-ene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\). Oxidative cleavage of the double bond yields an ethanal molecule from the two-carbon side (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)) and a propanal molecule from the three-carbon side (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CHO}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The resulting cleavage products match as: But-2-ene yields two moles of ethanal; 2-Methylprop-1-ene yields propan-2-one and methanal; Propene yields ethanal and methanal; and Pent-2-ene yields ethanal and propanal.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q10 - Match aromatic hydrocarbons with their ring system structures

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbon) List II (Structural Characteristic)
(A) 1,2-Benzanthracene (I) Two fused benzene rings (\(10\pi\) electrons)
(B) 1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene (II) Three angularly fused benzene rings (\(14\pi\) electrons)
(C) Naphthalene (III) Four fused benzene rings (carcinogenic hydrocarbon)
(D) Phenanthrene (IV) Five fused benzene rings (carcinogenic hydrocarbon)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural identification of 1,2-benzanthracene
1,2-Benzanthracene consists of an anthracene core (three linearly fused benzene rings) fused with an additional benzene ring at positions 1 and 2. It contains a total of four fused benzene rings and is recognized as a potent carcinogenic polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon.

Step 2: Structural identification of 1,2,5,6-dibenzanthracene
1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene consists of an anthracene nucleus fused to two additional benzene rings at positions 1,2 and 5,6. It possesses a total of five fused benzene rings and is cited as an important carcinogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon.

Step 3: Structural identification of naphthalene
Naphthalene is the simplest bicyclic benzenoid aromatic hydrocarbon, consisting of two benzene rings fused together in an ortho arrangement with a shared carbon-carbon bond, containing \(10\pi\) electrons.

Step 4: Structural identification of phenanthrene
Phenanthrene is an angular tricyclic benzenoid hydrocarbon composed of three fused benzene rings arranged in an angular (non-linear) orientation, containing \(14\pi\) electrons.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Correlating each hydrocarbon with its ring configuration: 1,2-Benzanthracene corresponds to four fused benzene rings; 1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene corresponds to five fused benzene rings; Naphthalene corresponds to two fused benzene rings (\(10\pi\) electrons); and Phenanthrene corresponds to three angularly fused benzene rings (\(14\pi\) electrons).
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q01 - Dihedral angle in eclipsed ethane conformation

questiontext.text: In the eclipsed conformation of ethane, what is the dihedral (torsional) angle in degrees between adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds on the two carbon atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecule: Ethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)).
Conformation: Eclipsed form.

Step 2: Assumptions and Reference Points
The dihedral angle (also called torsional angle) is defined as the angle between the planes formed by the front \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond and the rear \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond along the carbon-carbon single bond axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In an eclipsed conformation, bonds attached to the front carbon atom align directly in front of the corresponding bonds of the rear carbon atom.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because the front and rear \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds lie in exactly the same plane with zero angular displacement, the dihedral angle is \(0^\circ\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The dihedral angle in degrees is an exact non-negative value: \(0\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(0\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q02 - Number of pi electrons in benzene

questiontext.text: According to Hückel's rule, how many completely delocalised \(\pi\) electrons are present in the aromatic ring of benzene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Compound: Benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)).
Rule: Hückel's \((4n + 2)\pi\) electron rule of aromaticity.

Step 2: Assumptions and Reference Points
Benzene is a planar, monocyclic, fully conjugated ring system with \(n = 1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of delocalised \(\pi\) electrons is given by: \[N_{\pi} = 4n + 2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For benzene, substituting \(n = 1\): \[N_{\pi} = 4(1) + 2 = 6\] Each of the six \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atoms contributes one electron in an unhybridised \(2p\) orbital, giving a total of 6 \(\pi\) electrons.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total number of \(\pi\) electrons is an integer: \(6\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(6\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q03 - Dihedral angle in staggered ethane conformation

questiontext.text: In the staggered conformation of ethane, what is the dihedral (torsional) angle in degrees between adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds on the two carbon atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecule: Ethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)).
Conformation: Staggered form.

Step 2: Assumptions and Reference Points
The staggered conformation represents the arrangement in which the hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbon atoms are oriented as far apart from each other as possible.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In Newman or Sawhorse projections, the three bonds at each tetrahedral carbon are projected at \(120^\circ\) intervals. When staggered, the rear bonds bisect the \(120^\circ\) angle between the front bonds.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The angle of bisection between adjacent front and rear bonds is: \[\theta = \frac{120^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ\] Thus, the dihedral angle is \(60^\circ\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The angular separation in the staggered form is \(60^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(60\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q04 - Moles of oxygen for butane combustion

questiontext.text: Calculate the number of moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) required for the complete stoichiometric combustion of one mole of butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)). (Give your answer as a decimal number.)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Fuel: Butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)).
Amount of fuel: \(1\text{ mole}\).
Process: Complete combustion to \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Chemical Model
Combustion follows the general formula for acyclic alkanes: \[\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2} + \left(\frac{3n + 1}{2}\right)\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow n\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + (n + 1)\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For butane, \(n = 4\). The stoichiometric coefficient of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) is \(\frac{3n + 1}{2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(n = 4\): \[\text{Moles of } \mathrm{O}_2 = \frac{3(4) + 1}{2} = \frac{12 + 1}{2} = \frac{13}{2} = 6.5\text{ moles}\] Balanced equation: \[\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10} + 6.5\,\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + 5\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Carbon balance: \(4 = 4\). Hydrogen balance: \(10 = 5 \times 2 = 10\). Oxygen balance: \(6.5 \times 2 = 13 = 4 \times 2 + 5 = 13\). The stoichiometric value is \(6.5\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(6.5\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q05 - Total sigma bonds in buta-1,3-diene

questiontext.text: What is the total number of \(\sigma\) (sigma) bonds in a molecule of buta-1,3-diene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Compound: Buta-1,3-diene.
Structural formula: \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\).
Molecular formula: \(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_6\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Bonding Model
Every single bond comprises one \(\sigma\) bond. Every double bond comprises one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For an acyclic hydrocarbon containing \(N_C\) carbon atoms and \(N_H\) hydrogen atoms: \[N_\sigma = N_{\mathrm{C-H}} + N_{\mathrm{C-C}}\] Since the chain is acyclic, \(N_{\mathrm{C-C}} = N_C - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3\). The number of \(\mathrm{C-H}\) single bonds equals the number of hydrogen atoms: \(N_{\mathrm{C-H}} = 6\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds: \(2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6\).
- \(\mathrm{C-C}\) \(\sigma\) bonds: \(3\) (one between \(\mathrm{C1-C2}\), one between \(\mathrm{C2-C3}\), and one between \(\mathrm{C3-C4}\)).
- Total \(\sigma\) bonds: \[N_\sigma = 6 + 3 = 9\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total \(\sigma\) bonds \(= 9\). (There are additionally \(2\) \(\pi\) bonds).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(9\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q06 - Total structural chain isomers of pentane

questiontext.text: How many structural (chain) isomers exist for the alkane having the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{12}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecular formula: \(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{12}\).
Homologous series: Alkanes (\(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\) with \(n = 5\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Model
Structural chain isomers differ in the branching pattern of the carbon atom chain.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Construct all unique non-isomorphic carbon skeletons satisfying the tetravalency of carbon.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Unbranched 5-carbon continuous chain: Pentane (\(n\)-pentane), \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\).
2. 4-carbon chain with one methyl branch at position 2: 2-Methylbutane (isopentane), \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\).
3. 3-carbon chain with two methyl branches at position 2: 2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane), \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_4\mathrm{C}\).
Total number of structural chain isomers \(= 3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
No other carbon skeleton is possible for five carbon atoms. The count is \(3\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(3\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q07 - Moles of oxygen for benzene combustion

questiontext.text: Based on the stoichiometric equation for complete combustion of benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)), calculate the number of moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) consumed per mole of benzene burnt. (Give your answer as a decimal number.)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Hydrocarbon: Benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)), so \(x = 6\) and \(y = 6\).
Quantity of benzene: \(1\text{ mole}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Reaction Model
Combustion of any hydrocarbon \(\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y\) is given by: \[\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y + \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow x\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + \frac{y}{2}\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The required moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) per mole of \(\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y\) is \(x + \frac{y}{4}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(x = 6\) and \(y = 6\): \[\text{Moles of } \mathrm{O}_2 = 6 + \frac{6}{4} = 6 + 1.5 = 7.5\text{ moles}\] In fractional form, this equals \(\frac{15}{2}\) moles.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Balanced equation: \[\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6 + 7.5\,\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 6\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + 3\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\] Oxygen balance: \(7.5 \times 2 = 15\) atoms; products: \(6 \times 2 + 3 \times 1 = 15\) atoms. The final value is \(7.5\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(7.5\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q08 - Total bonds in an ethyne molecule

questiontext.text: What is the total number of covalent bonds (sum of all \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds) present in an ethyne (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\)) molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecule: Ethyne (\(\mathrm{H-C\equiv C-H}\)).
Molecular formula: \(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Bonding Model
A single bond consists of \(1\,\sigma\) bond. A triple bond consists of \(1\,\sigma\) bond and \(2\,\pi\) bonds.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total covalent bonds \(= N_\sigma + N_\pi\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds: \(2\) (one at each terminus).
- \(\mathrm{C-C}\) \(\sigma\) bond: \(1\) (axial overlap of \(sp-sp\) orbitals).
- Total \(\sigma\) bonds \(= 2 + 1 = 3\).
- \(\mathrm{C-C}\) \(\pi\) bonds: \(2\) (lateral overlap of mutually perpendicular unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals).
- Sum of all covalent bonds: \[N_{\text{total}} = N_\sigma + N_\pi = 3 + 2 = 5\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each carbon shares \(4\) pairs of electrons (one with \(\mathrm{H}\), three with \(\mathrm{C}\)). Total shared electron pairs \(= 1 + 3 + 1 = 5\) covalent bonds.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(5\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q09 - Total sigma bonds in a benzene molecule

questiontext.text: What is the total number of \(\sigma\) (sigma) bonds present in a molecule of benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecule: Benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)).
Ring geometry: Planar hexagonal ring consisting of six \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atoms.

Step 2: Assumptions and Bonding Model
Each \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond in the hexagonal ring possesses one \(\sigma\) bond formed by \(sp^2-sp^2\) overlap. Each \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond possesses one \(\sigma\) bond formed by \(sp^2-1s\) overlap.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total \(\sigma\) bonds: \[N_\sigma = N_{\mathrm{C-C}(\sigma)} + N_{\mathrm{C-H}(\sigma)}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Six-membered ring contains \(6\) carbon-carbon bonds: \(N_{\mathrm{C-C}(\sigma)} = 6\).
- Six hydrogen atoms attached to six carbon atoms: \(N_{\mathrm{C-H}(\sigma)} = 6\).
- Total \(\sigma\) bonds: \[N_\sigma = 6 + 6 = 12\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Benzene has 12 \(\sigma\) bonds and 3 \(\pi\) bonds (6 delocalised \(\pi\) electrons). The number of \(\sigma\) bonds is \(12\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(12\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q10 - Number of chlorine atoms added in gammaxane

questiontext.text: How many chlorine atoms are present in one molecule of benzene hexachloride (gammaxane or BHC) formed by the addition of chlorine to benzene under ultraviolet light?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction: Benzene reacting with chlorine gas under ultraviolet light at \(500\text{ K}\).
Product: Gammaxane (benzene hexachloride, BHC).

Step 2: Assumptions and Reaction Stoichiometry
Benzene undergoes free-radical addition across its three formal double bonds: \[\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6 + 3\,\mathrm{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{UV}/500\text{ K}} \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\mathrm{Cl}_6\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Three molecules of diatomic chlorine (\(3 \times 2 = 6\) chlorine atoms) add to one benzene ring.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The resulting molecular formula of gammaxane is \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\mathrm{Cl}_6\). Each of the six ring carbons bears one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom. Therefore, the total number of chlorine atoms per molecule is \(6\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\mathrm{Cl}_6\) indicates exactly \(6\) chlorine atoms.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(6\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q11 - Total structural isomers of molecular formula C6H14

questiontext.text: What is the total number of structural (constitutional) isomers possible for the saturated acyclic alkane having molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{14}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecular formula: \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{14}\).
Classification: Saturated open-chain alkane conforming to \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\) with \(n = 6\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Isomer Criteria
Only structural isomers (chain and positional) are counted; stereoisomers are not present in this set.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Systematically vary the length of the parent carbon chain and the positions of alkyl substituents.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. 6-carbon parent chain: \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (\(n\)-hexane).
2. 5-carbon parent chain with a methyl branch at position 2: \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2-methylpentane).
3. 5-carbon parent chain with a methyl branch at position 3: \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (3-methylpentane).
4. 4-carbon parent chain with two methyl branches at positions 2 and 2: \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2,2-dimethylbutane).
5. 4-carbon parent chain with two methyl branches at positions 2 and 3: \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2,3-dimethylbutane).
No other unique connectivity is possible for \(6\) carbon atoms.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total number of structural isomers is \(5\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(5\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q12 - Total structural alkene isomers of C4H8

questiontext.text: How many structural (constitutional) alkene isomers exist with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_8\)? (Do not include stereoisomers or cycloalkanes.)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecular formula: \(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_8\).
Compound class: Alkenes containing one carbon-carbon double bond.

Step 2: Assumptions and Isomer Rules
Only acyclic structural (constitutional) isomers are to be evaluated. Geometrical (stereoisomeric) variants like cis/trans are counted as one unique structural connectivity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Degree of unsaturation \(= 4 - \frac{8}{2} + 1 = 1\). For an acyclic alkene, this corresponds to exactly one \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Straight-chain with double bond at terminal position: \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3\) (But-1-ene).
2. Straight-chain with double bond at internal position: \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\) (But-2-ene).
3. Branched chain with double bond: \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\) (2-Methylprop-1-ene).
These represent the only three distinct structural connectivities.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total structural alkene isomers \(= 3\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(3\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q13 - Pi bond enthalpy in ethene double bond

questiontext.text: In an ethene molecule, the total carbon-carbon double bond enthalpy is \(681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), and the carbon-carbon single bond enthalpy in ethane is \(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). Taking the single bond enthalpy as the value for the \(\sigma\) bond, calculate the bond enthalpy of the \(\pi\) bond in ethene in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Carbon-carbon double bond enthalpy in ethene (\(\Delta H_{\mathrm{C=C}}\)): \(681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Carbon-carbon single bond enthalpy in ethane (\(\Delta H_{\sigma}\)): \(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
The double bond in ethene consists of one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond: \[\Delta H_{\mathrm{C=C}} = \Delta H_{\sigma} + \Delta H_{\pi}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The \(\pi\) bond enthalpy is isolated by: \[\Delta H_{\pi} = \Delta H_{\mathrm{C=C}} - \Delta H_{\sigma}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the equation: \[\Delta H_{\pi} = 681 - 348 = 333\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check: \(348 + 333 = 681\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). The calculated \(\pi\) bond enthalpy is \(333\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(333\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_NUM_Q14 - Number of pi electrons in naphthalene

questiontext.text: Naphthalene is a bicyclic aromatic hydrocarbon with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_{10}\mathrm{H}_8\). According to Hückel's \((4n + 2)\pi\) electron rule with \(n = 2\), how many delocalised \(\pi\) electrons are present in the naphthalene conjugated ring system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molecule: Naphthalene (\(\mathrm{C}_{10}\mathrm{H}_8\)).
Hückel integer value: \(n = 2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Model
Naphthalene is a planar, bicyclic, fully conjugated aromatic ring system containing ten \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atoms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Hückel's rule states that the number of delocalised \(\pi\) electrons in an aromatic system is: \[N_{\pi} = 4n + 2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(n = 2\) into Hückel's equation: \[N_{\pi} = 4(2) + 2 = 8 + 2 = 10\] In naphthalene, there are 5 conjugated double bonds in the resonance hybrid, contributing \(5 \times 2 = 10\) delocalised \(\pi\) electrons across the two fused rings.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each of the 10 \(sp^2\) carbons contributes 1 electron from its unhybridised \(2p\) orbital, yielding exactly 10 \(\pi\) electrons.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(10\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Sequence of free radical chlorination stages

questiontext.text:
Consider the photochemical chlorination of methane to form chloromethane. The reaction involves the following mechanistic events:

I. Attack of a chlorine free radical on a methane molecule to generate a methyl free radical and hydrogen chloride
II. Homolytic cleavage of the chlorine-chlorine bond by ultraviolet light to generate chlorine free radicals
III. Attack of the methyl free radical on a chlorine molecule to produce chloromethane and regenerate a chlorine free radical
IV. Mutual combination of active free radicals leading to chain termination

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these steps in the overall reaction mechanism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initiation Stage
The free-radical chain reaction begins with initiation. Under the influence of ultraviolet light (\(h\nu\)), the relatively weak \(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}\) bond undergoes homolysis to produce two reactive chlorine free radicals (\(2\dot{\mathrm{Cl}}\)). Therefore, homolytic fission of the chlorine molecule occurs first.

Step 2: Propagation - First Step
In the first chain-propagating step, a chlorine free radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane (\(\mathrm{CH_4}\)), breaking the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond and generating a methyl free radical (\(\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)) alongside \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

Step 3: Propagation - Second Step
The newly generated methyl free radical then attacks another chlorine molecule (\(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)), abstracting a chlorine atom to produce the principal product chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)) while liberating a new chlorine free radical (\(\dot{\mathrm{Cl}}\)) to sustain the chain.

Step 4: Termination Stage
Eventually, when radicals collide with one another without generating new reactive intermediates (such as two methyl radicals combining to form ethane, or a methyl radical combining with a chlorine radical), the free radicals are consumed and the reaction chain is terminated.

Step 5: Final Sequence Assembly
The chronological order of these events is: generation of chlorine radicals by homolysis (II), attack on methane to yield methyl radical (I), reaction of methyl radical with chlorine to form chloromethane (III), and combination of radicals for termination (IV).

Final Conceptual Answer: II → I → III → IV

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Industrial preparation stages of ethyne

questiontext.text:
On an industrial scale, ethyne is prepared starting from limestone (\(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)). Consider the following chemical transformations involved in this industrial process:

I. Hydrolysis of calcium carbide with water to produce ethyne and calcium hydroxide
II. Thermal decomposition of limestone to produce quicklime (\(\mathrm{CaO}\)) and carbon dioxide
III. High-temperature reduction of quicklime with coke in an electric furnace to form calcium carbide (\(\mathrm{CaC_2}\))

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these steps in the industrial synthesis of ethyne?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calcination of Limestone
The industrial synthesis of ethyne begins with the calcination of limestone (\(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)). Heating limestone causes thermal decomposition: \[\mathrm{CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaO + CO_2}\] This produces quicklime (\(\mathrm{CaO}\)).

Step 2: Formation of Calcium Carbide
In the second stage, quicklime is heated with coke (\(\mathrm{C}\)) in an electric furnace at high temperature: \[\mathrm{CaO + 3C \longrightarrow CaC_2 + CO}\] This produces calcium carbide (\(\mathrm{CaC_2}\)).

Step 3: Hydrolysis to Generate Ethyne
In the final stage, calcium carbide is treated with water at room temperature: \[\mathrm{CaC_2 + 2H_2O \longrightarrow Ca(OH)_2 + C_2H_2}\] This reaction liberates ethyne gas.

Step 4: Sequence Conclusion
The correct chronological order of the operations is thermal decomposition of limestone (II), followed by heating with coke to produce calcium carbide (III), and finally treatment with water to liberate ethyne (I).

Final Conceptual Answer: II → III → I

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Elementary steps in Kolbes electrolytic synthesis

questiontext.text:
During Kolbe's electrolytic synthesis of ethane using an aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate, the anodic process proceeds through several elementary stages:

I. Anodic oxidation of acetate ions by losing electrons to produce acetate free radicals
II. Complete electrolytic ionization of sodium ethanoate in aqueous solution to yield acetate ions and sodium ions
III. Dimerization (coupling) of two methyl free radicals to form an ethane molecule
IV. Spontaneous decarboxylation of acetate free radicals to eliminate carbon dioxide and form methyl free radicals

What is the correct logical and chronological sequence of these steps leading to the formation of ethane at the anode?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dissociation of Electrolyte
Before electrolysis takes place, sodium ethanoate dissolves and ionizes completely in water to generate sodium ions and acetate ions: \[2\mathrm{CH_3COONa \rightleftharpoons 2CH_3COO^- + 2Na^+}\] This ionization must occur first.

Step 2: Electron Transfer at the Anode
During electrolysis, the negatively charged acetate ions migrate to the anode, where they lose one electron each (oxidation): \[2\mathrm{CH_3COO^- \xrightarrow{-2e^-} 2CH_3COO^\bullet}\] This forms unstable acetate free radicals.

Step 3: Decarboxylation of the Radical
The acetate free radical is unstable and rapidly undergoes homolytic cleavage (decarboxylation) with the elimination of carbon dioxide gas to generate methyl free radicals: \[2\mathrm{CH_3COO^\bullet \longrightarrow 2\dot{C}H_3 + 2CO_2\uparrow}\]

Step 4: Radical Coupling
Finally, two methyl free radicals combine through radical coupling to form an ethane molecule: \[\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH_3\uparrow}\]

Step 5: Final Sequence Assembly
The chronological order of these steps is: electrolytic ionization (II), loss of electrons at the anode to form acetate radicals (I), decarboxylation to produce methyl radicals (IV), and coupling of methyl radicals to form ethane (III).

Final Conceptual Answer: II → I → IV → III

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Chronological steps in peroxide effect mechanism

questiontext.text:
The addition of hydrogen bromide to propene in the presence of benzoyl peroxide yields 1-bromopropane via a free-radical chain mechanism (Kharasch effect). Consider the following elementary steps:

I. Reaction of a phenyl free radical with hydrogen bromide to form benzene and a bromine free radical (\(\dot{\mathrm{Br}}\))
II. Addition of the bromine free radical to the terminal carbon of propene to generate a more stable secondary carbon radical
III. Homolysis of the peroxy linkage in benzoyl peroxide followed by spontaneous loss of carbon dioxide to yield phenyl free radicals
IV. Hydrogen abstraction from a second hydrogen bromide molecule by the secondary carbon radical to give 1-bromopropane and regenerate a bromine free radical

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Peroxide Dissociation and Decarboxylation
The reaction begins with the thermal homolysis of the weak oxygen-oxygen single bond in benzoyl peroxide: \[\mathrm{(C_6H_5COO)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2C_6H_5COO^\bullet}\] The resulting benzoyloxy radicals rapidly undergo decarboxylation to generate phenyl free radicals (\(2\dot{\mathrm{C}}_6\mathrm{H}_5 + 2\mathrm{CO_2}\)). Hence, this initiator cleavage occurs first.

Step 2: Generation of Bromine Radical
The highly reactive phenyl free radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from \(\mathrm{HBr}\) via homolysis to yield stable benzene and release an active bromine free radical: \[\dot{\mathrm{C}}_6\mathrm{H}_5 + \mathrm{H-Br} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \dot{\mathrm{Br}}\]

Step 3: Radical Addition to Propene
The bromine free radical attacks the \(\pi\)-bond of propene. Addition at the terminal carbon atom produces the more stable secondary carbon radical (\(\mathrm{CH_3-\dot{C}H-CH_2Br}\)) rather than the less stable primary carbon radical.

Step 4: Hydrogen Abstraction to Form Product
In the second propagation step, the secondary carbon radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from another \(\mathrm{HBr}\) molecule: \[\mathrm{CH_3-\dot{C}H-CH_2Br + H-Br \longrightarrow CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br} + \dot{\mathrm{Br}}\] This yields 1-bromopropane as the major product and regenerates a bromine free radical to propagate the chain.

Step 5: Final Sequence Assembly
The correct sequential order of steps is: initiator decomposition (III), generation of bromine radical (I), addition to alkene (II), and product formation with radical regeneration (IV).

Final Conceptual Answer: III → I → II → IV

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Mechanistic stages in electrophilic nitration

questiontext.text:
The electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism for the nitration of benzene using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid proceeds through distinct stages:

I. Proton transfer from sulphuric acid to nitric acid to produce protonated nitric acid and hydrogen sulphate ion
II. Abstraction of a proton from the \(sp^3\) hybridized carbon of the arenium ion by hydrogen sulphate ion to restore aromaticity
III. Dehydration of protonated nitric acid to generate the electrophilic nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO_2^+}\)) and water
IV. Electrophilic attack of the nitronium ion on the benzene ring to form a resonance-stabilized arenium ion (\(\sigma\)-complex)

What is the correct chronological sequence of these mechanistic stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Protonation of Nitric Acid
In the nitrating mixture, sulphuric acid acts as a stronger acid and protonates nitric acid, which behaves as a base: \[\mathrm{H_2SO_4 + HNO_3 \rightleftharpoons H_2\overset{+}{O}-NO_2 + HSO_4^-}\] This initial proton transfer generates protonated nitric acid.

Step 2: Generation of the Electrophile
The protonated nitric acid is unstable and dissociates by losing a neutral water molecule to generate the active linear electrophile, the nitronium ion: \[\mathrm{H_2\overset{+}{O}-NO_2 \rightleftharpoons H_2O + NO_2^+}\]

Step 3: Formation of the Arenium Ion (\(\sigma\)-Complex)
The electrophilic nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO_2^+}\)) attacks the \(\pi\)-electron cloud of the benzene ring. This slow, rate-determining step converts one aromatic \(sp^2\) carbon into an \(sp^3\) carbon, generating the non-aromatic, resonance-stabilized arenium ion (\(\sigma\)-complex).

Step 4: Proton Removal and Restoration of Aromaticity
In the final, rapid step, the base \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) abstracts the proton attached to the \(sp^3\) hybridized carbon of the \(\sigma\)-complex. The electron pair of the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond returns to the aromatic sextet, restoring aromatic resonance stabilization and producing nitrobenzene alongside \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).

Step 5: Final Sequence Assembly
The sequence of mechanistic events is: protonation of nitric acid (I), loss of water to form nitronium ion (III), attack of nitronium ion on benzene to form arenium ion (IV), and deprotonation to regenerate the aromatic ring (II).

Final Conceptual Answer: I → III → IV → II

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Synthetic sequence from 12-dibromoethane to benzene

questiontext.text:
A chemist converts 1,2-dibromoethane into benzene through a series of sequential chemical reactions:

I. Further dehydrohalogenation of bromoethene using strong base sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH_2}\)) to produce ethyne
II. Cyclic polymerization of ethyne by passing it through a red-hot iron tube at \(873\text{ K}\) to yield benzene
III. Base-induced elimination of one molecule of hydrogen bromide from 1,2-dibromoethane using alcoholic potassium hydroxide to form bromoethene

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of reactions for this laboratory synthesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: First Elimination Reaction
1,2-Dibromoethane is a vicinal dihalide. Heating it with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) causes \(\beta\)-elimination of one molecule of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to yield bromoethene (vinyl bromide): \[\mathrm{BrCH_2-CH_2Br \xrightarrow{alc.\ KOH} CH_2=CHBr + KBr + H_2O}\] This transformation must be carried out first.

Step 2: Second Elimination Reaction
Bromoethene contains a less reactive vinylic halogen due to resonance partial double-bond character. To eliminate the second molecule of \(\mathrm{HBr}\), a stronger base such as sodamide in liquid ammonia (\(\mathrm{NaNH_2}\)) is required: \[\mathrm{CH_2=CHBr \xrightarrow{NaNH_2} CH\equiv CH + NaBr + NH_3}\] This produces ethyne.

Step 3: Cyclic Trimerization
Finally, three molecules of ethyne undergo cyclic polymerization when passed through a red-hot iron tube maintained at \(873\text{ K}\): \[3\mathrm{CH\equiv CH \xrightarrow{Fe,\ 873\ K} C_6H_6}\] This cyclization yields benzene.

Step 4: Conclusion
The proper sequential order of the reactions is: mono-dehydrohalogenation using alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) (III), complete dehydrohalogenation using \(\mathrm{NaNH_2}\) (I), and cyclic trimerization in a red-hot iron tube (II).

Final Conceptual Answer: III → I → II

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Multistep synthesis of benzene from ethanoic acid

questiontext.text:
The complete textbook synthesis converting ethanoic acid (\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)) into benzene is structured into six key synthetic transformations:

I. Decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate by heating with soda lime (\(\mathrm{NaOH + CaO}\)) to produce methane
II. Photochemical chlorination of methane in the presence of diffused light to produce chloromethane
III. Dehydrohalogenation of chloroethane with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) to form ethene, followed by addition of bromine to yield 1,2-dibromoethane
IV. Neutralization of ethanoic acid with aqueous sodium hydroxide to yield sodium ethanoate
V. Sequential dehydrohalogenation of 1,2-dibromoethane to ethyne, followed by cyclic polymerization in a red-hot iron tube at \(873\text{ K}\) to produce benzene
VI. Wurtz coupling of chloromethane with sodium metal in dry ether to yield ethane, followed by monochlorination to chloroethane

What is the correct sequential order of these stages for the overall synthesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conversion to Salt
The synthesis begins with ethanoic acid (\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)). Neutralization with aqueous sodium hydroxide converts it to sodium ethanoate (\(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\)). Thus, stage IV is first.

Step 2: Decarboxylation
Heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime (\(\mathrm{NaOH + CaO}\)) causes decarboxylation, eliminating \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) and stepping down the carbon chain to yield methane (\(\mathrm{CH_4}\)). Thus, stage I follows IV.

Step 3: First Halogenation
Methane is subjected to free-radical monochlorination with \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) in the presence of light (\(h\nu\)) to synthesize chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)). Thus, stage II follows I.

Step 4: Carbon Chain Doubling
Treatment of chloromethane with sodium metal in dry ether (Wurtz reaction) couples two methyl units to form ethane (\(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\)). Subsequent monochlorination gives chloroethane (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\)). Thus, stage VI follows II.

Step 5: Formation of Unsaturated Intermediate
Heating chloroethane with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) produces ethene (\(\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}\)) via \(\beta\)-elimination. Ethene then reacts with bromine in carbon tetrachloride to form 1,2-dibromoethane (\(\mathrm{BrCH_2-CH_2Br}\)). Thus, stage III follows VI.

Step 6: Alkyne Formation and Cyclization to Benzene
1,2-Dibromoethane is converted to ethyne by successive treatment with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) and \(\mathrm{NaNH_2}\). Finally, passing ethyne through a red-hot iron tube at \(873\text{ K}\) achieves cyclic trimerization to form benzene. Thus, stage V completes the pathway.

Step 7: Final Sequence Assembly
The correct sequence is: IV → I → II → VI → III → V.

Final Conceptual Answer: IV → I → II → VI → III → V

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_SEQUENCING_Q08 - Analytical stages in alkene ozonolysis elucidation

questiontext.text:
Ozonolysis is an established analytical method used to determine the exact position of a double bond in an unknown alkene. Consider the following procedural and chemical stages:

I. Reductive cleavage of the cyclic ozonide intermediate with zinc dust and water (\(\mathrm{Zn / H_2O}\))
II. Electrophilic addition of ozone (\(\mathrm{O_3}\)) across the carbon-carbon double bond of the alkene to form an ozonide
III. Separation, isolation, and spectroscopic identification of the resulting carbonyl fragments (aldehydes and/or ketones)
IV. Deducing the connectivity and structure of the original alkene by conceptually removing carbonyl oxygen atoms and joining the carbonyl carbon atoms with a double bond

Which of the following represents the correct logical and chronological sequence of these operations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Ozonide Formation
The experimental analysis starts by passing ozone gas through a solution of the alkene in an inert solvent. Ozone adds across the carbon-carbon double bond to form an initial molozonide which rearranges into a stable, cyclic ozonide. Thus, ozonide formation (II) occurs first.

Step 2: Reductive Cleavage
The ozonide is then treated with zinc dust and water (\(\mathrm{Zn / H_2O}\)). Zinc acts as a reducing agent preventing aldehydes from being oxidized to carboxylic acids by hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)), cleaving the ozonide into smaller carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and/or ketones). Thus, stage I follows II.

Step 3: Identification of Fragments
The reaction mixture is worked up to isolate and characterize the specific aldehydes and ketones formed (for instance, identifying ethanal and propanone). Thus, stage III follows I.

Step 4: Structural Deduction
Finally, using the identified structures of the carbonyl products, the position of unsaturation in the parent alkene is deduced by placing the two carbonyl carbons face to face, removing the oxygen atoms, and joining those carbons with a double bond. Thus, stage IV concludes the analytical process.

Step 5: Final Sequence Assembly
The correct chronological order is: ozonide formation (II), reductive cleavage with zinc and water (I), identification of carbonyl fragments (III), and structural reconstruction of the parent alkene (IV).

Final Conceptual Answer: II → I → III → IV

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q01 - General molecular formula of alkane homologous series

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the general molecular formula for the open-chain alkane family (homologous series)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of alkanes
Alkanes are saturated open-chain hydrocarbons containing only carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single bonds.

Step 2: Examine homologous series members
Starting from methane (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\)) where \(n = 1\), ethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)) where \(n = 2\), and propane (\(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_8\)) where \(n = 3\), each successive homologue differs by a \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\) unit.

Step 3: Derive the general formula
For \(n\) carbon atoms, the number of hydrogen atoms required to satisfy carbon tetravalency in an open chain is \(2n + 2\). Thus, the general formula is \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The general molecular formula for acyclic alkanes is \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q02 - Geometry and bond angle of methane

questiontext.text: According to VSEPR theory, what is the spatial geometry and the \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angle in a methane molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the hybridisation of carbon in methane
In methane (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\)), the central carbon atom forms four equivalent \(\sigma\) bonds with four hydrogen atoms by head-on overlapping of \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals with hydrogen \(1s\) orbitals.

Step 2: Determine spatial geometry
Four equivalent electron pairs arrange themselves at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron to minimize mutual electrostatic repulsion.

Step 3: Evaluate the bond angle
In a regular tetrahedron with four identical bonded atoms and no lone pairs, all \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angles are exactly \(109.5^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Methane possesses a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of \(109.5^\circ\).

answer.text: Square planar geometry with bond angles of \(90^\circ\)
Trigonal pyramidal geometry with bond angles of \(107^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q03 - Historical origin of the term olefins

questiontext.text: Alkenes were historically known as 'olefins' because the first member of the series, ethylene, possesses which characteristic property?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the historical name of alkenes
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing carbon-carbon double bonds and were traditionally termed olefins, derived from the Latin words 'oleum' (oil) and 'facere' (to make).

Step 2: Identify the experimental basis
The lowest stable alkene, ethene (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4\)), reacts with chlorine gas to form an oily liquid product, ethylene dichloride (1,2-dichloroethane).

Step 3: Conclude the defining behavior
Because of the formation of an oily substance upon halogenation, ethene and its family members were named oil-forming or olefins.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Ethene forms an oily liquid product upon reaction with chlorine.

answer.text: It burns to produce oily residues without soot
It is extracted directly from olive oil
It forms an oily liquid product on reaction with chlorine

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q04 - Relative rate of alkane halogenation reactions

questiontext.text: What is the correct order of reactivity of halogens towards substitution reactions with alkanes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the halogenation process
Alkanes undergo free radical substitution when treated with halogens under light or elevated temperature.

Step 2: Examine halogen bond energies and activation barriers
Fluorine reacts violently and explosively even in the dark because of very low activation energy and highly exothermic steps. Chlorine reacts steadily in diffused sunlight. Bromine reacts more slowly and selectively. Iodination is exceptionally slow and reversible.

Step 3: Arrange in order of decreasing rate
The established rate of reaction decreases from fluorine to iodine: \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The order of reactivity of halogens towards alkanes is \(\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q05 - Chemical composition of soda lime reagent

questiontext.text: In the laboratory decarboxylation of sodium salts of carboxylic acids to yield alkanes, what is the chemical composition of 'soda lime'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the decarboxylation reaction
Heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime eliminates carbon dioxide as sodium carbonate, yielding an alkane with one carbon atom less than the parent acid.

Step 2: Recall the constituents of soda lime
Soda lime is prepared as an intimate dry mixture of sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{CaO}\)).

Step 3: Understand the role of calcium oxide
Calcium oxide keeps the strongly hygroscopic sodium hydroxide dry and allows solid-phase heating without melting the glass reaction vessel.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Soda lime is a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaO}\)).

answer.text: A mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaCl}_2\))
A mixture of sodium carbonate and calcium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{CaCO}_3\))
A mixture of sodium bicarbonate and quick lime (\(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3 + \mathrm{CaO}\))
A mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaO}\))

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q06 - Dihedral angle of eclipsed ethane conformation

questiontext.text: In the eclipsed conformation of ethane, what is the value of the dihedral (torsional) angle between adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds on the two carbon atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define dihedral angle
The dihedral or torsional angle is the angle of rotation about the carbon-carbon single bond measured between the planes containing the front \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond and the rear \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond.

Step 2: Analyse the eclipsed conformation
In the eclipsed conformation, the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds attached to the front carbon atom align directly in front of the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds of the rear carbon atom.

Step 3: Determine the angular value
Because the front and rear bonds lie in identical planes with no angular separation, the dihedral angle is \(0^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The dihedral angle in the eclipsed conformation of ethane is \(0^\circ\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q07 - Qualitative test for unsaturation using bromine

questiontext.text: What visible observation serves as a classic qualitative laboratory test for carbon-carbon unsaturation when an alkene is treated with bromine dissolved in carbon tetrachloride?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the unsaturation test reagent
Bromine in carbon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{Br}_2 / \mathrm{CCl}_4\)) has an intense reddish-orange colour.

Step 2: Trace the addition reaction
When an alkene is added, electrophilic addition takes place across the carbon-carbon double bond to form a colourless vicinal dibromoalkane.

Step 3: State the visible change
As the molecular bromine is consumed in forming the vicinal dibromide, the reddish-orange colour of the solution is completely discharged (decolourised).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Decolourisation of the reddish-orange bromine solution indicates the presence of unsaturation.

answer.text: Evolution of dense brown nitrogen dioxide gas
Discharge and decolourisation of the reddish-orange solution
Appearance of a persistent bright yellow flame

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q08 - Geometry and hybridisation of ethyne molecule

questiontext.text: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and the \(\mathrm{H-C-C}\) bond angle in an ethyne (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2\)) molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the electronic configuration and hybridisation
In ethyne (\(\mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)), each carbon atom forms one \(\sigma\) bond with hydrogen and one \(\sigma\) bond with the adjacent carbon atom using two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals.

Step 2: Examine remaining p-orbitals
The two unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals on each carbon overlap laterally to create two perpendicular \(\pi\) bonds.

Step 3: Determine geometry and bond angle
The two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals are directed linearly at an angle of \(180^\circ\) to each other, giving ethyne a linear structure with \(\mathrm{H-C-C}\) bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The carbon atoms in ethyne are \(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

answer.text: \(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(120^\circ\)
\(sp^2\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(120^\circ\)
\(sp\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\)
\(sp^3\) hybridised with a bond angle of \(109.5^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q09 - Addition of chlorine to benzene under ultraviolet

questiontext.text: When benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet light at \(500\text{ K}\), three chlorine molecules add to form a compound commonly known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reaction conditions
Benzene reacts with three molecules of chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)) under ultraviolet light or sunlight at \(500\text{ K}\) via a free radical addition process.

Step 2: Determine the product formula
The addition of six chlorine atoms across the three formal double bonds destroys the aromatic ring, yielding benzene hexachloride with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\mathrm{Cl}_6\).

Step 3: Identify the commercial name
This chlorinated cyclohexane derivative is known commercially as benzene hexachloride (BHC), Lindane, or gammaxane.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The product formed is benzene hexachloride, commonly termed gammaxane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q10 - Pi electron count of aromatic benzene ring

questiontext.text: According to Hückel's rule of aromaticity, how many delocalised \(\pi\) electrons are present in a neutral benzene ring corresponding to an integer value of \(n = 1\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State Hückel's rule
For a planar, cyclic, completely conjugated ring system to be aromatic, it must contain \((4n + 2)\) delocalised \(\pi\) electrons, where \(n\) is a non-negative integer (\(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)).

Step 2: Substitute the value of n
For the monocyclic system benzene with \(n = 1\): \[(4 \times 1 + 2) = 6\pi\text{ electrons}\]

Step 3: Verify with electronic structure
Benzene has six \(sp^2\) hybridised carbon atoms, each contributing one electron in an unhybridised \(2p\) orbital, forming a completely delocalised cloud of six \(\pi\) electrons.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Benzene contains \(6\pi\) delocalised electrons corresponding to \(n = 1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q11 - Boiling point trends of isomeric pentane molecules

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly lists the three structural isomers of pentane (\(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{12}\)) in decreasing order of their boiling points?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the isomers of pentane
The three isomeric pentanes are pentane (\(n\)-pentane), 2-methylbutane (isopentane), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).

Step 2: Understand the physical factor controlling boiling point
Intermolecular van der Waals attractive forces depend directly upon the surface area of contact between adjacent molecules.

Step 3: Evaluate the effect of branching
As branching increases, the molecular shape becomes increasingly spherical and compact. A sphere has the minimum surface area per unit volume, which reduces the contact area and weakens the intermolecular van der Waals forces.

Step 4: Compare experimental boiling points
Pentane has an unbranched open chain and boils at \(309.1\text{ K}\). 2-Methylbutane has one branch and boils at \(300.9\text{ K}\). 2,2-Dimethylpropane has two branches (spherical symmetry) and boils at \(282.5\text{ K}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The decreasing order of boiling points is pentane > 2-methylbutane > 2,2-dimethylpropane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q12 - Origin of ethane byproduct in methane chlorination

questiontext.text: During the photochemical chlorination of methane, a small amount of ethane is formed as a byproduct. Which elementary step in the free radical chain mechanism accounts for this observation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Review the free radical halogenation mechanism
The mechanism involves three distinct stages: chain initiation, chain propagation, and chain termination.

Step 2: Examine the radicals generated during propagation
In propagation step (a), a chlorine free radical abstracts hydrogen from methane: \(\mathrm{CH}_4 + \dot{\mathrm{Cl}} \rightarrow \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + \mathrm{HCl}\), producing methyl free radicals (\(\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)).

Step 3: Examine chain termination pathways
Termination occurs when two free radicals combine with each other, consuming active radicals without generating new ones.

Step 4: Identify the specific coupling step
The combination of two methyl free radicals, \(\mathrm{H}_3\dot{\mathrm{C}} + \dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), forms ethane as a chain-terminating byproduct.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Coupling of two methyl free radicals in a chain termination step yields ethane.

answer.text: Attack of a chlorine radical on a dichloromethane molecule during propagation
Direct reaction between two methane molecules stimulated by ultraviolet light
Combination of two methyl free radicals in a chain termination step
Homolytic cleavage of a carbon-hydrogen bond in chloromethane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q13 - Stoichiometry of complete alkane combustion reaction

questiontext.text: Based on the general combustion equation for alkanes, how many moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) gas are required for the complete stoichiometric combustion of one mole of butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the general alkane combustion equation
The complete balanced combustion of any alkane is given by: \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2} + \left(\frac{3n + 1}{2}\right)\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow n\,\mathrm{CO}_2 + (n + 1)\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Identify the value of n for butane
For butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)), the number of carbon atoms is \(n = 4\).

Step 3: Calculate the oxygen coefficient
Substitute \(n = 4\) into the stoichiometric oxygen coefficient: \[\frac{3(4) + 1}{2} = \frac{12 + 1}{2} = \frac{13}{2} = 6.5\]

Step 4: Verify with chemical equation
\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}(\mathrm{g}) + \frac{13}{2}\,\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4\,\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 5\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\). Exactly \(\frac{13}{2}\) (or 6.5) moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) are consumed.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Complete combustion of one mole of butane requires \(\frac{13}{2}\) moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q14 - Controlled catalytic oxidation of methane to methanol

questiontext.text: What major product is obtained when methane and dioxygen are heated in a \(2:1\) molar ratio in the presence of a copper tube catalyst at \(523\text{ K}\) and \(100\text{ atm}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify controlled oxidation reactions of methane
Controlled oxidation of methane yields different products depending on the catalyst and reaction conditions.

Step 2: Evaluate the copper catalyst conditions
When a mixture of methane and oxygen is passed through a copper tube at \(523\text{ K}\) under a pressure of \(100\text{ atm}\), controlled partial oxidation takes place: \[2\,\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}/523\text{ K}/100\text{ atm}} 2\,\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}\]

Step 3: Distinguish from molybdenum oxide catalyst
Heating with molybdenum oxide (\(\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) produces methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)), whereas copper produces methanol.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Controlled oxidation of methane over copper at \(523\text{ K}\) and \(100\text{ atm}\) yields methanol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q15 - Selective permanganate oxidation of tertiary alkanes

questiontext.text: Although alkanes are generally resistant to chemical oxidising agents, 2-methylpropane is oxidised by potassium permanganate (\(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\)) to form:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the structural features of 2-methylpropane
The structure of 2-methylpropane is \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH}\). It contains three primary methyl groups and one tertiary carbon bonded to a single tertiary hydrogen atom.

Step 2: Recall the reactivity of tertiary C-H bonds towards oxidation
Alkanes ordinarily resist oxidation by common aqueous reagents, but a tertiary hydrogen atom is relatively reactive due to lower bond dissociation energy and greater stability of intermediate species.

Step 3: Identify the oxidation product
Potassium permanganate specifically oxidises the tertiary \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond into a tertiary alcohol: \[(\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO}_4} (\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{OH}\] The resulting compound is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Oxidation of 2-methylpropane with potassium permanganate produces 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q16 - Aromatization of hexane to benzene derivatives

questiontext.text: When \(n\)-hexane is heated to \(773\text{ K}\) under a pressure of \(10\text{--}20\text{ atm}\) in the presence of supported oxides of chromium, vanadium, or molybdenum, which conversion occurs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reaction type
Heating an open-chain alkane possessing six or more carbon atoms at elevated temperature and pressure over transition metal oxide catalysts supported on alumina is known as aromatization or reforming.

Step 2: Trace the chemical transformations
The process involves two consecutive steps: dehydrogenation (loss of hydrogen molecules) followed by ring closure (cyclisation).

Step 3: Determine the product from n-hexane
For \(n\)-hexane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3(\mathrm{CH}_2)_4\mathrm{CH}_3\)), cyclisation and loss of four hydrogen molecules results in the formation of the aromatic compound benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Dehydrogenation and cyclisation of \(n\)-hexane produces benzene.

answer.text: Complete oxidation to produce carbon dioxide and water
Thermal cracking to form propene and propane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q17 - Energy barrier and torsional strain of ethane

questiontext.text: Rotation around the carbon-carbon single bond in ethane is hindered by an energy barrier of approximately \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\). This barrier arises predominantly from which factor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define the conformational energy barrier in ethane
The staggered conformation of ethane has lower potential energy than the eclipsed conformation by approximately \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Analyze the source of instability in the eclipsed form
In the eclipsed conformation, the electron clouds of adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds are brought into closest proximity with zero dihedral angle.

Step 3: Identify the strain phenomenon
The repulsive interaction between adjacent bonding electron pairs is termed torsional strain. It is maximized in the eclipsed form and minimized in the staggered form.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The energy barrier in ethane is due to repulsive interactions between adjacent bonding electron clouds, known as torsional strain.

answer.text: Steric hindrance between large bulky alkyl substituent groups
Electrostatic attraction between opposite formal charges on carbon atoms
Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding between ethane molecules
Repulsive interactions between electron clouds of adjacent \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bonds (torsional strain)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q18 - IUPAC nomenclature of conjugated diene hydrocarbons

questiontext.text: What is the correct IUPAC name of the branched diene having the structural formula: \[\mathrm{CH}_2 = \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)=\mathrm{CH}_2\]?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the parent conjugated diene
The longest continuous carbon chain containing both double bonds consists of four carbon atoms. The parent diene is buta-1,3-diene.

Step 2: Identify and number substituents
Numbering from either end gives the double bonds at locants 1 and 3, and two methyl substituents at locants 2 and 3.

Step 3: Combine prefix and parent chain
The complete systematic IUPAC name is 2,3-dimethylbuta-1,3-diene.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The IUPAC name of the compound is 2,3-dimethylbuta-1,3-diene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q19 - Counting sigma and pi bonds in buta-1,3-diene

questiontext.text: How many sigma (\(\sigma\)) bonds and pi (\(\pi\)) bonds are present in a molecule of buta-1,3-diene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds
Buta-1,3-diene has molecular formula \(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_6\). Each hydrogen atom forms a single covalent \(\sigma\) bond with carbon, contributing \(6\) \(\mathrm{C-H}\) \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 2: Count carbon-carbon sigma bonds
The linear four-carbon backbone \(\mathrm{C}_1-\mathrm{C}_2-\mathrm{C}_3-\mathrm{C}_4\) contains \(3\) carbon-carbon \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 3: Sum total sigma bonds
Total \(\sigma\) bonds = \(6\,(\mathrm{C-H}) + 3\,(\mathrm{C-C}) = 9\) \(\sigma\) bonds.

Step 4: Count pi bonds
Each carbon-carbon double bond contains one \(\pi\) bond. With two double bonds (at \(\mathrm{C}_1=\mathrm{C}_2\) and \(\mathrm{C}_3=\mathrm{C}_4\)), there are \(2\) \(\pi\) bonds.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Buta-1,3-diene contains 9 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q20 - Structural requirements for alkene geometrical isomerism

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds is capable of exhibiting geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State conditions for geometrical isomerism
An alkene exhibits geometrical isomerism if rotation about the double bond is restricted and each doubly bonded carbon atom is attached to two different atoms or groups (i.e. \(\mathrm{XYC=CXY}\), \(\mathrm{XYC=CXZ}\), or \(\mathrm{XYC=CZW}\)).

Step 2: Examine propene
In propene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) bears two identical hydrogen atoms; hence no geometrical isomerism is possible.

Step 3: Examine 2-methylprop-1-ene
In \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) has two hydrogens and \(\mathrm{C}_2\) has two methyl groups; no cis-trans isomerism is possible.

Step 4: Examine but-1-ene
In but-1-ene (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)), \(\mathrm{C}_1\) bears two identical hydrogen atoms; cannot show cis-trans isomerism.

Step 5: Examine but-2-ene
In but-2-ene (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), each double-bonded carbon is bonded to one \(-\mathrm{H}\) and one \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\). This allows two distinct spatial configurations: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: But-2-ene satisfies the structural requirements and exhibits cis-trans isomerism.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q21 - Dipole moment difference in but-2-ene isomers

questiontext.text: The dipole moment of cis-but-2-ene is \(0.33\text{ D}\), whereas that of trans-but-2-ene is almost zero. What is the fundamental reason for this difference?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the polarity of individual bonds
In but-2-ene, \(sp^3\) hybridised methyl carbons are less electronegative than \(sp^2\) hybridised doubly bonded carbon atoms, generating bond dipole vectors directed from \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) toward \(=\mathrm{CH}-\).

Step 2: Evaluate vector addition in the trans isomer
In trans-but-2-ene, the two \(\mathrm{C-CH}_3\) bond dipoles point in directly opposite directions across the double bond. Their vector sum cancels out completely, resulting in a net dipole moment of zero.

Step 3: Evaluate vector addition in the cis isomer
In cis-but-2-ene, both \(\mathrm{C-CH}_3\) bond dipoles are oriented on the same side of the double bond, reinforcing each other to produce a net resultant dipole moment of \(0.33\text{ D}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: In the trans isomer, the two bond dipole moments point in opposite directions and cancel each other, whereas in the cis isomer they reinforce each other.

answer.text: The cis isomer contains stronger covalent bonds than the trans isomer
In trans-but-2-ene the bond dipoles are in opposite directions and cancel, while in cis-but-2-ene they reinforce each other
The cis isomer undergoes rapid spontaneous ionisation in the liquid phase
The trans isomer has higher resonance stabilisation that quenches polarity

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q22 - Stereoselective cis hydrogenation using Lindlar catalyst

questiontext.text: When an internal alkyne such as but-2-yne is partially reduced with dihydrogen in the presence of Lindlar's catalyst, which stereoisomeric product is predominantly formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define Lindlar's catalyst
Lindlar's catalyst consists of palladised charcoal (\(\mathrm{Pd}/\mathrm{C}\)) that has been partially deactivated ('poisoned') with substances such as quinoline or sulphur compounds.

Step 2: Examine the catalytic surface mechanism
Deactivation prevents further reduction of the alkene to an alkane. Dihydrogen adds to the alkyne from the metallic surface via syn-addition (both hydrogen atoms add from the same side of the triple bond).

Step 3: Determine product geometry
Syn-addition of two hydrogen atoms to but-2-yne yields cis-but-2-ene as the stereoselective product.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Partial reduction using Lindlar's catalyst yields cis-alkenes stereoselectively.

answer.text: An equimolar mixture of cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q23 - Stereoselective trans alkene synthesis via sodium ammonia

questiontext.text: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium metal in liquid ammonia (\(\mathrm{Na} / \text{liquid } \mathrm{NH}_3\)) stereoselectively yields which type of alkene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the Birch-type reduction of alkynes
Treatment of an alkyne with sodium in liquid ammonia involves dissolving metal reduction via single electron transfer steps.

Step 2: Analyze the intermediate geometry
Transfer of electrons forms a radical anion intermediate that adopts the trans configuration to minimize electrostatic and steric repulsion between the lone pairs/substituents.

Step 3: Determine product stereochemistry
Subsequent protonation yields the thermodynamically more stable trans-alkene stereoselectively.

Final Conceptual Conclusion: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium in liquid ammonia produces a trans-alkene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q24 - Reactivity trends in dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides

questiontext.text: During the \(\beta\)-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of alkyl halides with alcoholic potash (\(\text{alc. } \mathrm{KOH}\)), what are the correct reactivity orders with respect to the nature of the halogen atom and the alkyl group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the nature of dehydrohalogenation
Alkyl halides heated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) eliminate a molecule of hydrogen halide (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) to form an alkene via \(\beta\)-elimination.

Step 2: Evaluate the leaving group ability of halogens
The carbon-halogen bond strength decreases down the halogen group: \(\mathrm{C-I} < \mathrm{C-Br} < \mathrm{C-Cl}\). Iodide is the best leaving group, making the rate order: \(\text{iodine} > \text{bromine} > \text{chlorine}\).

Step 3: Evaluate the stability of transition state across alkyl groups
Elimination from tertiary alkyl halides forms more highly substituted and stable alkenes, and proceeds through lower activation energy. The rate order for alkyl groups is: \(\text{tertiary} > \text{secondary} > \text{primary}\).

Final Conceptual Conclusion: The reactivity orders are iodine > bromine > chlorine for halogens, and tertiary > secondary > primary for alkyl groups.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS11_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q25 - Dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides using zinc

questiontext.text: What product is formed when 1,2-dibromopropane is heated with zinc dust in alcohol?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classify 1,2-dibromopropane
1,2-Dibromopropane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CHBr}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)) contains two bromine atoms on adjacent carbon atoms, making it a vicinal dihalide.

Step 2: Examine the dehalogenation reaction
When treated with zinc metal, vicinal dihalides undergo dehalogenation with the elimination of a molecule of zinc halide: \[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHBr}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br} + \mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2 + \mathrm{ZnBr}_2\]

Step 3: Identify the hydrocarbon product
The resulting alkene is propene.
